subtopic: FORTY-MINUTE RULE INTERPRETATION OF STANDING ORDER 37-REPLY TO MOTION OF WANT OF CONFIDENCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FORTY-MINUTE RULE INTERPRETATION OF STANDING ORDER 37-REPLY TO MOTION OF WANT OF CONFIDENCE
speechtext:
I wish to take this occasion to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, a point of order concerning the discussion on the budget. I shall at once admit that it can have no bearing on the present discussion, but I think the point is of sufficient importance to warrant my bringing it up now, because I would not wish that the procedure followed be cited as a precedent for future discussions without having the point finally decided by the chair, I refer to an incident which took place on June 4. After the hon. member for Sheliburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), speaking for the official opposition, had discussed the budget resolutions and exercised his right under standing order 37 to speak for more than forty minutes, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) followed, and when his forty minutes had expired, the hon. member for

Forty-Minute Rule
Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) directed the attention of the chair to the fact that the minister had spoken for forty minutes. I do not think Your Honour was in the chair at the time, but it was decided that the minister was quite within his right to follow up the debate for more than forty minutes, and without any grounds being given or any rule cited, the Minister of Trade and Commerce was allowed to continue. I submit that in that case there was a misinterpretation of standing order 37, and I do so not in the least spirit of animosity but merely because I think the house will agree it is very important that the rule be decided by Your Honour for future guidance in budget debates.
I shall read standing order 37 and endeavour to show that the decision as rendered was not according to the rule. Standing order 37 reads:
No member, except the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, or a minister moving a government order and the member speaking in reply immediately after such minister, or a member making a motion of "no confidence" in the government and a minister replying thereto, shall speak for more than forty minutes at a time in any debate.
I admit the rule may be confusing, but let me point out that there are three exceptions to the provision that members shall not speak for more than forty minutes. In the first place the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition may speak for more than forty minutes. In the second place a minister moving a government order and a member speaking immediately in reply after such minister may speak for more than forty minutes. In the third place a member making a motion of no confidence in the government and a minister replying thereto may speak more than forty minutes. It is evident that the third exception was interpreted as applying to the budget debate, but the budget debate, in my opinion, comes under the second exception. The Minister of Finance rises in his place and moves the house into committee of ways and means to consider certain resolutions which constitute a government order. The Minister of Finance thus moves a government order and the member immediately replying on behalf of the opposition may speak for more than forty minutes. But because another minister happens to follow in the debates, he has not also the right to expand the limit beyond forty minutes. The Minister of Finance, in opening the debate, places before the house a government order. He also has the right to close the debate after every hon. member has been given an opportunity to speak. But because casually another minister follows the official critic of
the opposition, that minister certainly does not come under standing order 37. The third exception provided for does not apply to the budget which is a positive government order moved by the Minister of Finance. It applies to a motion for committee of supply, where a member on this side moves an amendment and the minister who is involved in that amendment is allowed an opportunity of replying for more than forty minutes. But when we come to the budget, it would seem both unfair and not according to the standing order that after the Minister of Finance has spoken at length and the official critic of the opposition has also spoken at length, another minister just because he happens to follow, can also exceed the forty-minute rule.
I admit that I am raising that point a little late, but, I said, it is very important because the procedure followed may be cited as a precedent governing future debate. Therefore I would ask Your Honour not to rule on the point to-day, but to consider it and to give a written decision after careful study so that we may know where we stand in the matter.

But, on the other hand, any amendment to the motion to go into committee of ways and means has always been considered a want of confidence motion.

speechtext:
Please let me finish my
statement. My hon. friend may speak after me. It is a time-honoured custom both in supply and ways and means to move votes of want of confidence in the government, and that is done simply by moving an amend-
Forty-Minute Rule

ment to the motion to go into committee of supply or ways and means. A government may or may not accept this as a motion of want of confidence, but it is a motion of want of confidence all the same. That being the case, a minister who replies immediately after the mover of that motion is, under this standing order, entitled to unlimited time. No other hon. member would have that privilege, but the rule distinctly says that a minister replying immediately after the mover of a motion of want of confidence is unlimited in regard to his time. I do not express any opinion as to the propriety of the rule, but there the rule is, and having regard to the strict letter of the rule and parliamentary custom in the house and in England, I submit the ruling was correct as the standing order is now framed, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not limited as to time.

subtopic: FORTY-MINUTE RULE INTERPRETATION OF STANDING ORDER 37-REPLY TO MOTION OF WANT OF CONFIDENCE
speechtext:
I think there is a great deal of truth in what the Minister of Justice points out. This all arises from the change that was adopted a few years ago. Under an old interpretation by one of the first Speakers in the Canadian parliament after confederation-Mr. Blanehet, I think-it was decided, contrary to what was practised in England, that on a motion to go into supply or ways and means there could be only one amendment, and that became the practice in this parliament. In fact, I was taught the advantages of that practice by my old friend Sir Wilfrid Laurier once when I wanted to bring in a motion against the government, and he told me how to do it, against his own government, which I thought was very nice of him. Under the old practice there was no doubt that the amendment submitted as against the motion to go into supply or ways and means had to be voted on before the main motion was taken up, but in the session of 1927-28, the last time the rules were revised, the rules were extended and it was decided that a subamendment could be moved after an amendment had been moved to a motion to go into supply or ways and means. As the rules have been framed, somewhat hastily, the interpretation of the Minister of Justice is correct. But I think it is nonsensical all the same. If the amendment moved by one member of one group or another is to be interpreted as a motion of want of confidence whatever it contains, then why should the mover of a subamendment be treated differently from the mover of an amendment. I think that is an important point.
There is one point in what the Minister of Justice said to which I desire to take exception, namely, that an amendment to go into supply or ways and means is of necessity a motion of want of confidence. Contrary to my habit, I interrupted the Minister of Justice to point out that that interpretation has been raised frequently, and one has only to refer to Bourinot, for example, to find out that that interpretation is not correct. In fact, there comes to my memory just now a very striking incident under the old Conservative government. I think it was Mr. Costigan who brought up a motion of sympathy with Ireland in her struggle for home rule on the motion to go into supply.

Riviere du Loup Station

Mr. Dafoe wrote his book at the time Laurier was living, and in it I have found two introductory and suggestive lines of poetry which I think I might quote at this time:
Ne'er of the living can the living judge;
Too blind the affection or too fresh the
grudge.
I think those two lines might very well apply to some hon. members opposite when we come to sizing up statesmen and public men. My plea, Mr. Speaker, at this time is for a wider conception of the duties of statesmanship and for a wider sympathy for leaders of all parties. I believe if we get that we will have a higher class of politics in this Canada of ours-something to be devoutly desired. The book of Mr. Dafoe dealt with the character, capacity, leadership and contributions made by Laurier, the great Liberal leader, to Canada. So in this book of Senator John Lewis we find that the senator deals in a capable manner with the character, the ability, the capacity, the leadership and the remarkably fine contribution made by the right hon. leader of the opposition to the building up of a greater dominion.
At this time I wish only to outline a running sketch to tell hon. members of this house that the right hon. leader of the opposition graduated, like many other eminent Canadians, from the public schools of the province of Ontario, that he is a graduate from the university of Toronto, a postgraduate student of the university of Chicago, a student in the post-graduate school of
Harvard university. At both Chicago and at Harvard alike he had won post-graduate fellowships, at Harvard he won as well a travelling fellowship which took him for a year in 1899 to the continent of Europe. His studies throughout his secondary school and public school and university courses, both under-graduate and post-graduate showed him at all times to be-

speechtext: Is this a biography?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext:
Partly. Why not? If
my hon. friends will allow me to proceed they may ask as many questions as they like later on. I was saying that the right hon. leader of the opposition possessed unusual political capacity. That is one reason for his great success. Some of the hon. members opposite otherwise equipped would undoubtedly like to possess a similar capacity, but it is quite obvious that such a capacity is wanting. He also evinced as a student a special interest in political affairs and had the habit ever of a real investigator of the truth. Not only that but, like his paternal grandfather who was skilled in gunnery and military engineering, the right hon. leader of the opposition is also skilled in political gunnery and enveloping flank movements, as hon. members opposite only too well realize.
After the right hon. leader of the opposition finished his post-graduate course in Chicago, he returned to Canada and was responsible for investigating certain public contracts in this country and bringing about minimum wage legislation, which has proved to be a very important aid to labour. Then he visited Europe to continue his studies. In 1900 he became Deputy Minister of Labour, organizer of the labour department and founder of the Labour Gazette, with which we are all familiar. During his term as deputy minister he went ahead and courageously settled forty labour disputes, of which the following are examples:
The southern Alberta coal mines dispute in 1906, and an industrial dispute in the cotton factories of Quebec in 1908.
To emphasize what I have been discussing, Mr. Speaker, may I quote the opinion of Doctor Charles W. Eliot, president emeritus of Harvard university, respecting the ability of the right hon. leader of the opposition in the adjustment of labour troubles. Doctor Eliot said:
When one considers all the activities of the Department of Labour at Ottawa before and since the enactment of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, one sees clearly that the Canadian action on the labour problem has been and still is the most intelligent and successful in the world. It shows one safe way at least towards industrial peace.

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh
The Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King invented this legislation and got it put into effect.
The leading ideas which appear in his writings, speeches and political career are that governmental investigations should precede the lockout or the strike in order to bring law and order into industry and to introduce joint control. Secondly, that the government should pass laws effective in uncovering wrongs and exposing injustice in industrial controversies, and that if the community is to pay regard to the rights of labour and capital on the one hand, labour and capital on the other must not be . indifferent to the well-being of the community; and thirdly, that the methods of preserving peace between nations are similar to those that obtain in industry, namely, conciliation, arbitration and the international support of a judicial tribunal whose decisions are enforceable by an international police.
Later, in 1908, the right hon. gentleman became Minister of Labour. In 1914 he became connected as a specialist with the Rockefeller foundation, but remained in Canada directing the work of research into industrial relations from Ontario, his native province. His connection with this institution was indirectly referred to yesterday by the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion). I have before me the latest report of the foundation, and hon. members may be interested to learn what it is doing right now in Canada. At page 370, under the title "Canada," I find the Rockefeller foundation is giving aid to further these important activities:
Aid to local health departments; aid for research; epidemiology; fellowships; McGill university; university of Montreal; nursing surveys and visits; public health training station, Beauce county; school of hygiene and public health, Toronto; study of veterinary education and research; visits and surveys by medical staff members; visits of teachers and administrators; Canadian national committee for mental hygiene.
At page 168 I find that $262,500 was given to schools and institutes of hygiene and public health in Toronto. At page 20 I find that the University of Toronto secured $10,000, and at page 17 it appears that the Canadian National Committee for Mental Hygiene, Toronto, received $29,700; at page 15 I find that McGill university received $15,000, the University of Montreal $25,000 and Dalhousie university $7,000. I do not think I need go further to show the importance of the Rockefeller foundation in encouraging the work of health education in Canada. It was the industrial research branoh of the foundation that my right hon. leader was appointed director of. In other words, the direction of this branch of its activities required a man who knew its business-not a mediocrity or a tail man, but an outstanding man; and therefore the foundation got him from Canada. I think we should consider it a

great honour that any native son can be chosen within the boundaries of Canada to fill such an important position, for he not only adds lustre to his own community and to his own province, but also to the dominion of which he is an outstanding representative.
Now, we might as well know what this organization did to further the war efforts of Great Britain and the allied nations early in the struggle and later. It was the first organization in the United States to come to the relief of the Belgians with food and clothing and of the starving people in France, Poland, Serbia and Armenia; it contributed millions of dollars to Red Cross and Y.M.C.A. work; it equipped war demonstration hospitals; in peace its activities were confined to medical education and public health; it maintained industrial peace during the war and so brought about the maximum production of munitions. In this latter work it helped Canada to play her full part in the world war.

I will conclude my quotation:
-which was proposed by you, and in the operation of which, since its installation, we have had the benefit of your frequent advice. Indeed, I feel that the part you have had in the establishment of the new and better relationships in our industry represents a contribution to the late war of inestimable value. I can consistently so express myself, because I had some misgivings as to the wisdom of the course you laid out for us, and am now convinced it has exceeded the most sanguine expectations expressed at its beginning.
I know hon. gentlemen opposite do not like to listen to statements of this kind, still I am going to quote them. They need them. May I put on Hansard a statement by the vice-president of the Bethlehem Shipbuilding Corporation, which during the war employed 70,000 men. It is as follows:
At the time we asked for assistance, there was a great deal of unrest among our labour, and we believe that the advice you gave us was of material assistance in reducing this unrest and in correspondingly increasing the efficiency in the production of ships. As this company is far and away the largest ship-building concern in the world, and as it produced a very large percentage of all the ships actually completed in this country during the period of its participation in the war, i.e., something like sixty per cent of the destroyers, and over twenty per cent of the merchant craft, your assistance was evidently of real value from the standpoint of helping to win the war.
How do you like that? My right hon. leader became in 1919 head of the Liberal party in Canada, and I might say, Mr. Speaker, that as head of successful Liberal governments from 1921 to 1930 he showed such capacity for leadership, such vision of statesmanship and such anxiety to cope with all problems of concern to Canada that as head of that party to-day he has 'the unanimous support, the outstanding loyalty and the love of every Liberal in Canada.
I might just read what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said about Sir John A. Macdonald when he was laid to rest; when we read this we can better come to our own conclusion with regard to some of the desperately small and insignificant statements made against our leader by the heads of the Tory party in Canada, who work themselves up to stark frenzy every time we have an appeal to the country. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, when we read it we think more of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, we think of him

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh

aa a real man and a Canadian just as when we read some of the statements of hon gentlemen opposite we think less of them. The time has come for plain speaking in this house, and I am going to do some of it. I might say that as far as Sir Wilfrid Laurier was concerned, I stood by him through thick and thin. I even stood by him in 1917, when many people thought he was wrong, but I am satisfied to-day, even more than I was at that time, that he pursued the only course he could pursue looking to a greater dominion. He stood for conscription of men and for conscription of wealth. If we. had conscripted wealth, Mr. Speaker, we would have had a billion or two billion dollars less of war debt hanging over this country to-day, and I would say that $2,000,000,000 would take care of a great deal of unemployment at the present time and put Canada absolutely on its feet. That is just a passing reference with regard to how the finances of Canada were handled in the past, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not at the helm. If I have time to-day I desire to deal specifically with Canadian finance and tariffs from 1867 onward.
To return to what I began to say, Sir Wilfrid Laurier had such faith in himself that he never refused to give to an opponent all the credit due him. Take his eulogy of his greatest political opponent, Sir John A. Macdonald. Standing before the grave of him who was by far the greatest father of confederation he said:
Let not our grief be barren grief but grief coupled with the resolution and the determination that the work in which Brown and Macdonald, Liberal and Conservative, united, shall and will live forever.
That is what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said about his political opponent, Sir John A. Macdonald, and I would say, Mr. Speaker, that I hope the time is not far distant when we can produce political heads and public leaders in Canada who at least can be sympathetic to their rivals and at the same time true to Canada, the empire and the rest of the world.
Now I should like to congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister upon the presentation of his first budget in the House of Commons. I am not satisfied with its contents, by any means; I do not think hon. members opposite or the people of Canada are satisfied, with it, and I believe hon. gentlemen opposite will hear from the people later on about the budget of 1931. It reminds me of a story, Mr. Speaker. A medical student had just graduated and was undergoing an examination or, as it is called, being put through his paces by a superior; he was being tested out, as it were. His professor said, "Now, you

are going out into the great world to practise your profession. Supposing some day you were at a place where an accident happened; supposing a gun powder explosion took place, a man was blown into mid air, and you were the only doctor present. What would you do?" The student said, "I would wait for him to come down". So, Mr. Speaker, we waited month after month and week after week, for the budget to be brought down and at last the budget came down. It has not come down or penetrated entirely into the minds of the people yet, but it is getting there gradually and I am more sorry for hon. gentlemen opposite the further it gets down or within the mental grasp of the people. When it was in thin air; while it was in the mind of the leader of the government and parliament had not its hands on it, it mhy have been all right, but it is not all right now for the hon. gentlemen opposite.
We find in the budget the different changes in the tariff and taxation brought down by the government at the present time. I would say the budgets of the late Hon. Mr. Robb were simple, brief, penetrating and compact. The budget of last year possessed clarity of vision; the arrangement of the material was satisfactory, and the new fiscal ground it covered was pointed out in a sensible way. With regard to the present budget I would say, Mr. Speaker, that it is too long; it is rather loosely jointed. The presentation of the budget in Hansard does not show a good make-up.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Won't you be a little
charitable?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I am always so,
I would say, that the Prime Minister in connection with that budget showed hard work. He is a hard worker; he showed determination; he showed courage. These are fine qualities, but although he showed these qualities and typified to a certain degree the spirit of Can-adianism I would say the budget after all is very unsatisfactory.
As far as the outstanding features of that budget are concerned they are something like the picture which comes before a traveller crossing the prairies, when he sees the mountains in the distance. He first sees the snowcapped peaks of the Rockies. These peaks, I would say remind one of the budget, of the high peaks of taxation and protection which bulge out hero and there from the first line of it to the last. Not only does he see the peaks of the mountains in the distance, but in a general view of the mountains he sees also the great masses of prehistoric rock which hold up

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh
these peaks which make them possible, when we come to the budget we also see something akin to these great masses of rook, though not nearly as solid, namely the great masses of words, sentences, paragraphs, campaign promises and policies of a protectionist nature, all indicating that the work of the Conservative party before the election, during the election and since the election has been to advance against the interests of the masses the doctrine of high protection. Then beyond the mountains the traveller views the somewhat clear sky, indicating the impossible ambitions, the perfervid visions and the ideals held out by the Conservative party last year, when they said over and over again that if the people voted for the Tory party everything would be all right, and then beyond the mountains in the darkening firmament, what is noticeable? Is there not a sky filled with threatening clouds which indicate the doubts, the suspicions and the fears that the people now have of the party which promised them so much and gave them so little? More than that, Mr. Speaker, as the traveller comes up close to the mountains he finds here and there modifying agencies like rushing rivers, lakes and tumbling streams. These indicate as far as the budget is concerned, the modifying agencies of duty and responsibility which have come to hon. gentlemen opposite during the last eight months. They are modifying them considerably. They are now quite subdued and timid, they are in doubt as to their policies; they do not know where they are at. The great valleys surrounding the mountains indicate the depressions-the immense gap-in public business, in public finance and in national trade; how economic conditions have gone all to pieces, as it w'ere, under the regime of hon. gentlemen opposite. We should not be surprised at this, when we find that the budget, in a protectionist way, puts duties upon the follow-ipg-these are but a few of the necessities of life taxed. The list is an enormous one.
Duties are being placed on beef, veal, lamb, mutton, canned meats, poultry, extracts of meat and fluid beef; on quail, partridges and squabs, dead or alive; on rabbits, frozen, when used for feeding foxes; and on preserved meats, either as bacon, hams or pork. This government has covered almost everything in the way of meats.
The old duty on tea was 7, 10 and 10 cents; last year it was reduced and made free, nine and 10 cents; nothing was done at the special session but now it is being made four, eight and eight cents and 10, 10 and 10 cents. Every cup of tea will now cost more. The old duty on rice, cleaned, per hundred pounds, 22110-1761
was 50, 65 and 75 cents, and it has been raised to 50 cents, 90 cents and one dollar. A duty has been placed on prepared vegetables, such as beans, baked or prepared, corn, tomatoes and peas, dried, desiccated, pickled or preserved. Protection has been placed against plums, dried prunes, raisins, dried currants, dates, figs, oranges, lemons, jellies, jams, marmalades, preserves, apricots, peaches, pears and pineapples. Added duties have been placed on spraying and dusting machines, grading machines and pruning machines, as well as on building supplies such as building and paving brick. A man cannot build a house without being taxed to death. Flagstones, sandstone and building stone are taxed along with marble and granite, rough, partly rough, plain, manufactured or partly manufactured. A duty has been placed on common and colourless window glass and laminated glass. All forms of clocks have been taxed. Protection has been, placed against field seeds such as timothy, clover and bent grass. Root and garden seeds, such as mangel, parsley, parsnips, turnip, cabbage, radish, cucumber, lettuce, carrot, cauliflower, celery, onion, pepper and tomato. The previous rates on furniture such as house, office and store furniture of wood, iron and other materials were 20, 27i and 30 per cent, but they have been changed by this blackest of budgets to 20, 30 and 45 per cent. Other household requirements such as dolls, toys, buttons, brushes, pens, penholders, rulers, lead pencils, crayons and clothespins have been protected. A duty has been placed upon belting, leather, sole leather, East India kip, glove leather, leather garments and manufactures of leather. Duties have been raised upon woven fabrics, whole or in part silk. Musical instruments are protected, such as phonographs, gramophones- this should interest hon. members opposite- and parts thereof, such as cylinders, records and mechanical piano and organ players.
The budget discloses that sporting goods of all kinds are to be taxed, A man will be unable any more to play a game of golf or baseball without being taxed. This tax covers such items as racing shells, racing oars, trawls, trawling spoons, fly hooks, sinkers, swivels, fishing reels, fishing rods, bait and hooks, fishing tackle, walking sticks and canes, golf clubs, skis, baseball hats and racquets. Pruning shears, dehorning instruments and sterilizing apparatus are being taxed. These should stir all horned and high protectionists opposite.
Anthracite coal is put at free, 40 and 40 cents per ton; coke, free, $1, and $1 per ton; coal screenings or coal dust, 35, 75 and 75 cents per ton; charcoal, free, $7.50 and $7.50 per ton, and bituminous coal, 75 cents per
The Budget-Mr. McIntosh

ton. Protection is provided also on iron and steel goods. The free items mentioned mean nothing to the consumers or users of these commodities or products.
When we come to the free list we find such articles as hospital and operating apparatus, but these items were free under the Liberal regime. Then we have printing machinery, but this item also was free under the Liberal regime. Also glass eyes for human use, and I commend that to hon. gentlemen opposite.
There is' one phase of the sales tax to which I would call attention. School books used by our boys and girls in the public and separate schools of Canada are being taxed, which means a tax on education and mental development. This may suit the Tory party but it certainly does not suit the Liberal party. We believe that the books used in our schools should be made as cheap as possible, and I ask hon. gentlemen opposite, the cabinet and the Prime Minister that this item be given the fullest consideration. The sales tax should be removed root and branch from the public school books of Canada.
A statement appears in the budget speech in connection with wheat, reading as follows:
We therefore propose to provide that the freight rates shall be adjusted by this country absorbing five cents per bushel on all wheat that is exported of the crop of this year. That provision is effective this year. That amount is taken into consideration in the estimates I have given of the expenditures for the year.
The first thing which should be cleared up by the government and by the Prime Minister is just what is meant by that five cent proposition. Who gets the five cents?

speechtext: Mackenzie King.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, he did not insert it in the budget. The real five centers, as usual when it comes to helping the farmers, are the leaders of this friendly multi-millionaire government. I submit that every farmer who ships a bushel of wheat should receive that five cents; I do not believe that only the farmer who ships export wheat should get it. It should apply to every farmer who ships wheat and coarse grain; if it is given only to the man who ships wheat it will affect only the wheat areas and not apply to the mixed farming areas of western Canada or other parts of the dominion. That should be changed so that every farmer will receive five cents per bushel for every bushel of wheat shipped for export and also for non-export. I hope the farmers of western Canada will not fall for this sop of protection. I do not believe the farmers and producers will fall

for this because the high protection policy is taking 31 to 33 cents out of every dollar they have, and five cents per bushel in return does not amount to very much. I say to the western farmers and producers, and to all of Canada: Be on the alert, size up clearly and definitely the policies of the Conservative party and do not let them put over a policy which will spell ruin and non-development for the three prairie provinces and the rest of the country.
My time is drawing to a close, but I would like to conclude with a comment upon the problem of finance as the basis of righting war debts, reparations and tariff trade barriers. The Prime Minister of Great Britain, Premier MacDonald, along with the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Philip Snowden, and the foreign minister, Hon. Arthur Henderson, recently met representatives of Germany to discuss the question of international finance. After this meeting the following statement was issued:
Both parties were agreed that in addition to efforts and measures of a national character, the revival of confidence and prosperity depended upon international cooperation. In this spirit both governments will endeavour to deal with the present crisis in close collaboration with the other governments concerned.
That means that there must be close collaboration among the European countries, and out of this will come that international action and cooperation so necessary for the revival of European trade and commerce. Then this European movement will spread to this continent and Canada will have to play her part in directing aright the financial reconstruction of the world.
Complementary to this question of international finance is that of higher and higher tariffs-now so dangerously high as to have brought about a condition of economic nationalism rather than that of universalism, without which all quack fiscal remedies will bring about a dangerous trade and credit breakdown throughout the world. I should like to put on Hansard what Sir George Paish, the eminent British economist say3 about this question.

speechtext:
During the last two weeks we
have listened to a great number of speeches from our hon. friends opposite; we have heard many things from them, but I think I can safely say to-day that so far nothing very important has been said against the budget now under discussion and that no really strong and serious objections have been

The Budget-Mr. Duranleau
raised against it. I say this even after the long speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and after the very interesting speech that has just been delivered by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh). What we have heard during the debate are only expressions along party lines under the rules of what we call the game of politics. But this is a first class budget and one point at least which my hon. friends opposite have to accept is that it contains a general policy which was accepted by the people at the last election.
If we go outside the house, we shall realize that there is an almost unanimous opinion that we have before us to-day the most comprehensive budget that has been presented to the house for many years. According to the issue of June 6 of the Financial Times of Montreal:
To all intents and purposes it is a business man's effort to take care of a national deficit of $75,000,000.
This budget is clear and definite, and I shall ask those who come forward with the declaration that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) had gone too far to remember, as the hon. member who has just resumed his seat said a minute ago, that the Prime Minister and his cabinet have been elected on a policy of tariff protection. It is true, as the hon. member said, that we spoke during the last election not of higher protection, but of sufficient protection, but to-day we are putting into acts the very proposals that we laid before the people and that have been accepted by a great majority of the electorate.
We have now only one thing to do: wait for results, and on that we confidently rely. Of course we have heard some recriminations from certain sources. This was to be expected. There is no doubt that nobody likes taxation. This government likes taxation less than anybody else, but as was said by the Vancouver Sun:
While some people feel good to-day, others distinctly do not, and it is all in the manner in which the Bennett tariff revisions strike their particular business.
There is no doubt that tariff makers are bound to step on somebody's toes, and some people have corns. May I add that after the speeches to which we have listened from hon. members opposite, there seem to be corns also on that side. But one must bear in mind that in the matter of budgeting, we have to consider not party politics, not the game of politics, but the first business of all, namely, the business of the country. The cabinet has also to defend the greatest and most sacred
of all causes, the cause of this motherland of ours. That means that we have to take good care of all fields of national activity: agriculture, manufacturing, industry, development of natural resources; in a word, everything that goes to increase the pay of the workingman and the bank account of the producer. I claim that that is what is undertaken by the budget now under discussion. But of course we shall have to meet conflict between those who have tendencies toward free trade and those who believe in protection, the former promising the country lower prices for commodities but with insufficient and sometimes no money to pay for them, and the latter arguing rightly, I suggest, that even high prices are sometimes beneficial when there is plenty of money to pay for the goods.
In that connection, it may be well to point out that we still have, in Canada, people who appear to think that large imports of manufactured or of agricultural goods are a sign of national prosperity. This is what the Calgary Herald has to say in this regard:
They are ready to ignore the fact that busy Canadian factories mean more work for Canadian workmen, and that national well-being cannot be fostered by sending out of the country every year hundreds of millions of dollars for goods that can be made just as well at home.
But what is this budget if it is not a determined effort for the development of the country along lines of self-preservation? Let me quote the Financial Post of Toronto of June 4 of this year. While complaining of some of the new schedules of the tariff it has this to say on the policy it reflects as a whole:
The policy of the government in endeavouring to build up Canadian industries and Canadian institutions for the benefit of the Canadian people by direct methods is strongly in evidence in the budget, although the increases in the tariff are not so great as had been generally expected. Certain branches of the steel, textile, woodworking and other manufacturing industries receive more protection, and there are further safeguards in the case of "dumping" of foreign products.
At the same time the agricultural industry benefits by increased duties on a number of farm products, including live hogs, fresh meats, dairy products, fruits and vegetables. The tendency to build up Canadian institutions is further made evident in the heavy taxes placed on premiums of British and foreign insurance companies.
Perhaps I may be allowed to quote from another paper, the Star of Vancouver, which is well known to our friends representing the city of Vancouver. As we all know, this paper is not very sympathetic to this government. After mentioning the problems whieh have had to be solved within a few months by this government, the Star says:
The Budget-Mr. Duranleau

Mr. Bennett has had problems of this sort in mind for many months past.	He has
wrestled with their complexities.	He has
finally attempted to solve them in the best interests of the country as a whole. And since his has been a sincere effort, based on his fundamental convictions, he has earned the thanks of Canada to-day, even though criticism begin to-morrow.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, to-morrow has come to an end and criticism has had its way in this house for over two weeks. I dare say, Mr. Speaker, that no hon. gentleman opposite, not even the leader of the opposition, with his four and five cent speech-I beg pardon, four hour and five minutes speech-has so far brought forward any sound and constructive suggestions, either to improve the situation or to improve the means of improving the situation.
As I said in the beginning of my remarks, public opinion in this country is almost wholly in favour of the budget now under discussion. Public bodies, outstanding business men and financial papers, are almost at one in commendation of what is now known, and justly known, as the Bennett budget. A survey of this country I am sure would disclose everywhere, not so much a love for taxes because nobody likes taxes, and this government less than anyone, but a real willingness on the part of the people to make a determined and common effort for the restoration of contentment and prosperity in this country. I would call that a real sentiment of cooperation. It is the cooperation that has been invited by the Prime Minister since he has been empowered with that great trust which was accorded to him by the people of Canada on the 28th of July last. As I said a moment ago, public 'bodies, outstanding business men and financial papers in this country are almost at one in commending this budget. May I now be allowed to quote a few opinions from our neighbours across the line, and from some in the old country. But first let us hear from Montreal, our great metropolis, and the greatest grain-distributing centre on this continent.
Among the opinions expressed by the leading citizens of Montreal none is more striking than the one expressed by Mr. Charles Duquette, ex-mayor of Montreal and presently the president of the ohamibre de commerce of Montreal. Speaking on June 3, Mr. Duquette, approving the sales tax and the budget revisions as a whole, said:
I am confident that the revisions announced in the budget will bring back prosperity by protecting all lines of industry, that they will procure work for everyone wishing to work, and that they will increase the purchasing power of individuals and of the community.

Speaking of one industry in particular, that of leather, Mr. Paul Galibert, an outstanding business man and leather manufacturer of Montreal and, by the way, a good Liberal, said:
An increased tariff on leather will revive the almost stagnant leather business. It cannot increase the price of leather.
Approval of the budget has come from both the east and the west. In British Columbia we have heard the manufacturers assembled in convention at Victoria express their belief that the new one per cent excise tax will not only raise a large revenue for Canada, between $15,000,000 and $25,000,000 per year in their estimation, but will also stimulate the production of raw materials and encourage manufacturing. But apart from the quotations that I have just made, I think that, perhaps the most just appreciation of the effect of the budget may be found in the comments that have been made by our neighbours on the other side of the line because, as we know, it is they, the United States, that will suffer most from the results of our tariff revision. What do they say about it? I desire to give only a few extracts, and first a despatch from Washington to the newspapers, dated June 3:
The Democrats and the low-tariff politicians characterize the action of the government of Prime Minister R. B. Bennett as retaliation against the Hawley-Smoot Tariff Act which two years ago raised the schedules of the United States to the highest point in history.
Let me add, Mr. Speaker, that the supporters of the United States tariff denied that assertion, and in that they are supported by a public declaration which was made by the Prime Minister of Canada not long ago.
I proceed. Chairman Jouett Shouse, of the Democratic national executive committee, said:
We can make no complaint to Canada, for we set the fashion of levying embargo duties. Canada frankly states that her purpose is to attract American investors so they will manufacture goods for Canadians in Canada.
Representative Collier, Democrat, of Mississippi, is of the same opinion. He says:
Canada is forcing American manufacturers, particularly steel and automobile producers, to go to Canada and set up plants, if they are to continue to supply that market.
Chairman Shouse-I quote him again- charged that through the Hawley-Smoot act "normal business of the United States with Canada is cut in half." Probable effects in dollars and cents upon exports from the United States to Canada have been calculated by American experts. A rough estimate indicated that from $100,000,000 to $150,000,000 worth of United States trade would suffer.

The Budget-Mr. Duranleau
Senator Lafollette, Republican-Progressive from Wisconsin, who opposed the Hawley-Smoot bill, said:
Canadian action will contribute to the already alarming decreases in American exports.
Senator Couzens, Republican, of Michigan, describes the Canadian increases as "an effort to aid Canadian fanners, and not retaliation." This all sounds very good, Mr. Speaker. I wish, however, to quote an extract from a Washington despatch dated June 3, two days after the presentation of the budget. This despatch addressed to the New York Times, reads as follows:
The revision, according to Doctor Klein-
The Assistant Secretary of Commerce,
-was inevitable if Canada was to retain its protectionist policy and equalize employment irregularities which have become accentuated in recent months with the further recession of industrial activity in the dominion.
His statement follo-wed indications given by Secretary of State Stimson earlier in the day that the United States would make no protest against the new Canadian tariff rates.
Mr. Stimson remarked that for years the United States as a general proposition had insisted that the tariff was a domestic matter for the country which imposed it, and that the state department had so asserted repeatedly in answer to foreign inquiries and protests concerning its tariffs. There would have to be some extraordinary features in a foreign tariff, he said, to make the United States break its own rule with any good face.
For two reasons I have read the last quotation to the house, first, to show that official circles in Washington admit the justification for our tariff revisions and, secondly, to reassure certain hon. members-who, after hearing the speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition, and I am afraid there are some who still require reassurance-express fear at the very idea of asserting our commercial rights before a powerful neighbour.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I shall refer to another point, that of our consideration of imperial interests in the drafting of the budget. Owing to the fact that the Imperial economic conference which was to take place this summer in Ottawa has been postponed to a later date I believe the consideration of this matter is of some importance. Hon. members will recall that the Prime Minister and his colleagues who went abroad to attend the Economic conference were assailed by our hon. friends opposite concerning the attitude they had taken in England. If I remember correctly, my hon. friends opposite took strong exception to some of the statements made in London by the Prime Minister. Up to date the right hon. leader of the opposition has stated that on those
occasions the Prime Minister was speaking not in the name of Canada but in the name of the Conservative party. The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), the former Minister of Justice, stated in this house he was glad that the Prime Minister in London had not spoken in the name of Mr. Lapointe and his friends. Well, I concede to my hon. friends opposite the right to dissociate themselves from any important undertaking which involves Canada and her empire trade. I might add that the fact that they watched from our shores the work of the Imperial economic conference was not a calamity so far as Canada is concerned. But I wish to emphasize the fact that the attitude of the government as expressed in the present budget has shown conclusively to the whole empire the sincerity of the Bennett proposals in England as well as our earnest desire to help to build on a mutually advantageous basis a larger empire trade. If our attitude is so well understood by our neighbours and by public opinion in London how is it that it seems not to be understood in this house? On this point I should like to quote another American opinion. Doctor Klein, to whom I have already referred makes the following statement:
It is obvious from a study of the commodities involved-
Speaking of our new tariff schedule.
-that a considerable portion of the increases has been made in preparation for the coming conference on reciprocal tariffs among the British dominions, which is to take place next fall. Canada is obviously and quite naturally putting herself in a favourable position for these negotiations.
Now let us see what the British opinion is on this subject. I have before me a Canadian Press despatch from London published by the Sun of Vancouver on June 3, 1931, under the title: "London Opinions." The despatch is as follows:
"The attitude of Canada toward empire trade is more than a gesture, says the Financial Times to-day in referring to the Canadian budget.
"The fact that tariff alterations are made so as to affect only in minor degree the British preference throws into relief the reality of the attachment of the Canadian statesmen to the idea of imperial development, the Financial Times continues.
"Canada Looks Ahead" is the heading of the Morning Post leader on the budget.
"Any doubt regarding Canada's power of recuperation should be dispelled by the triumphant success of her recent conversion scheme."
That is a London opinion, nothwithstand-ing opinions which have been expressed concerning the conversion loan by hon. members opposite. The article continues:
The Budget-Mr. Duranleau

What chiefly impresses the Morning Post in the budget is, first, its courageous facing of facts and next its persistence in the policy of preference for British goods.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with some other important questions relating to the budget. I shall turn first to the promises which were made by the Conservative party during the last election campaign and the fulfilment up-to-date of those promises. As my time is very limited however there is another question with which I should like to deal; I refer to the tactics employed during the last election campaign by the Liberal party, the Grit party in the province of Quebec. Throughout this debate we have been told many times that the Conservative party during the campaign of July, 1930, spoke too much of butter and of unemployment. Mr. Speaker, we spoke concerning those questions because they were real questions of fact and real questions at issue before the electors. We referred to unemployment because at that time the state of unemployment in our country was worse than it is now.

Yes, worse than it is now, in spite of our friends' regrets. The Liberals in Quebec were denying by telegrams, which have lately been repudiated by the premier of Quebec, that there was any question of unemployment in that province, when its then and present premier knew perfectly well that he was one of the greatest factors in that unemployment. Now, Mr. Speaker, they have resorted to these tactics for years in order to keep their grip on the province of Quebec, although that province has always been protectionist. I should like to refer to a speech made last Sunday by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Desroehers) when he stood beside the premier of Quebec. Mr. Taschereau is introducing into the campaign for the impending provincial general elections those questions which are issues in the federal field. What was said by the hon. member is almost incredible, Mr. Speaker, and he should be called upon before this house to substantiate what he then said. I propose to quote the speech as reported in Le Devoir. It was heard by the people of Quebec over the radio and I think it is a shame for any member of this house to have so spoken. He said:
Following the principle of economy, Mr. Bennett has suppressed the autos of the ministers. I have passed recently by the federal garage in Ottawa, and I have found that there were no automobiles. Where are those vehicles,
I Mr. Duranleau.]
have I asked? The ministers have gone out with them, was the answrer.
To compensate that suppressed privilege Mr. Bennett will increase by $2,000 the annual treatment of the ministers so as to allow them to pay for the expenses of their automobiles.
And listen to this, Mr. Speaker:
They will continue, I am sure, to use the automobiles they had before and which the government does not want to sell, and that is Mr. Bennett's way of practising economy.

Another of the tactics followed by the Grit party in Quebec at the last election was the revival of the old war scare. Two days before the voting, Le

Soleil, the official organ of the Grit party published the following:
London, the "Bleus," the war.

How many of my friends opposite would be at home to-day if such a cry had not been broadcast two days before the election? For those who were returned by small majorities it looks Like "stolen goods." What about the member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) who was elected by a few votes? What about the member for Yamaska (Mr. Boucher), who was elected by one vote? And what about other members on the Liberal side who were returned by very small majiorities and whom I have not time to mention? In great Britain they are looking for a Conservative victory

Will hon. members kindly note this:
-they are looking for a Conservative victory in Canada so that war against Egypt and India could be undertaken.
The house will note the suggestion that the British people could not declare war against India and Egypt unless the Conservative party in this country was victorious Major Newman says "England will be forced to have recourse to military measures. The subject will be discussed by the next Imperial conference. Whom shall we send to London?" That is how the question was put before the electors of the province of Quebec by the Liberal organizers

"Whom shall we send to London?" they asked. These comments should be inquired into in order to discover where that cablegram came from. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have liked very much to show my usual courtesy to the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) and commend him on his maiden speech in this house, if he had adopted a different tone. Lest I be understood as endorsing in the least anything he has said, I will at once withdraw any compliments I had contemplated uttering when he first rose.
The Minister of Marine, in his initial words, made the extraordinary statement that although he had listened to this debate for a number of days, he had heard nothing important with regard to the budget and that nothing of any significance had been advanced by any hon. member who had spoken. He even included the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), who made such a wonderful speech the other day, a speech which I am sure the country has read with great interest. I do not know what the Minister of Marine had in mind in making a statement of that kind; I think the budget has been assailed both by Liberals and by Progressives. That statement reminds me very much of a well known character in Quebec, a late member of the legislature, who fell into the habit of making statements such as that made by my hon. friend. This gentleman would appear at meetings and would be accused of everything under the sun. Then he would rise and merely say, "Well, you see, Mr. Chairman, they have nothing against
The Budget-Mr. Rinjret

me, only a few insignificant passing remarks. Therefore I will not bother to answer what has been said."
I will not say the same with regard to the speech of the Minister of Marine. I think, if only because of the impudence of certain of his statements and the inaccuracy of others, his speech is indeed very important. I regret that I am not moving a motion of want of confidence, or replying as a minister, because I would require much more than forty minutes to reply to everything the minister said, and I am afraid if I endeavour to do that I will have to neglect the notes I prepared very carefully in order to say something important myself with regard to the budget.
Let me point out, however, the very extraordinary situation in which the Minister of Marine has placed himself. He has heard the tariff, taxes, and many other features of the budget discussed by the most prominent members of this house, but he has found nothing important in what they have said. When he rises in this place to discuss the budget, however, he speaks of everything except the budget itself. He discusses automobiles and wars and everything else except the budget with which he thought we had dealt so lightly in the past few days. The Minister of Marine then went on and said the government had implemented in this budget every promise made during the last campaign. I may have time later on to go into certain details of the budget, but let me say right now that if the Prime Minister instead of going around the country promising everything, had gone before the country in July, 1030, and merely submitted this budget to the electorate of Canada, not only would this government not be in power but I dare say very few hon. gentlemen opposite would have been returned to parliament. The Prime Minister promised that he would end unemployment at once. The Prime Minister promised that he would put an end to agricultural distress. The Prime Minister promised that he would relieve the common and modest people from the burden of taxation under which they were sweating. The Prime Minister promised old age pensions to the extent of 100 per cent. The Prime Minister promised railway branch lines, and said that those who would travel on them would not have to pay very large fares. The Prime Minister promised bridges and said that those who passed over them would not have to pay tolls. The Prime Minister promised anything; he promised moonbeams and prosperity for this country, so I say that if instead of doing
[Mr. Rinfret.l
that he had told the people he was going to raise the sales tax from one per cent to four
per cent; that he was going to impose a one per cent tax on all the imports of this country; that he was going to do that most infamous thing, relieve himself and his wealthy friends of 25 per cent of their income tax, not only would be not have won the election but in certain parts of the country he would have been stoned away from his meetings.
Then, after saying we have offered no criticism to the budget, the Minister of Marine went on to say that while he had no time to prove it, the budget implements the promise of last year. With all the respect of which I am capable I say that is one of the most childish things I have ever heard in this house. The minister says, "Oh, of course there are taxes in the budget, but we do not like taxes. The government do not like taxes." I should say, from what we have seen in the income tax schedules, that at least the Prime Minister does not like taxes when they are [DOT]imposed upon himself. I am not concerned; I am not a millionaire and I do not expect to become a millionaire. I am a newspaper man; I do not belong to a class which usually possesses great fortunes in this world, but for once I regret that I am not a millionaire for I will say that this budget makes it very attractive for anyone to be a millionaire in this -Country.
Instead of giving his own oipinion about the budget, the Minister of Marine went on to give a series of quotations, very likely clipped for him by one of his secretaries, and he was astonished to find that there were some people [DOT]in this country and the United States who liked the budget. For instance, he quoted the opinion of former Mayor Duquette of Montreal, and apparently he was surprised to learn that he likes the budget. He forgot to add that ex-Mayor Duquette is a staunch Conservative; if there is one man in the province of Quebec who is likely to swallow anything coming from a Conservative government, certainly it is Mr. Duquette. Then he went on bo quote a leather merchant; he was also surprised to find that this gentleman, who trades in leather, is perfectly satisfied with the -protection he will get in his business. What an extraordinary situation. You protect leather, and the leather merchants say that is all right. Really that is a great discovery, and I congratulate my hon. friend upon making it. Then, to my great surprise my hon. friend, although belonging to this government, went across the border and quoted opinions from the nation to our south, the United States. He went along and quoted a

The Budget-Mr. Rinjret
large number of them, and whilst he was doing that there was still resounding in my ear the voice of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) who only a couple of days ago said that the policy of the Liberal opposition was not Canada first, but Washington first. How did the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) dare to quote American opinions? Probably he did so because the Minister of Railways was not in his seat. I venture to say that at the next council meeting an explanation will pass between these two ministers upon that very question.
The minister went on and ventured the opinion that unemployment in Montreal had decreased. We cannot be definite on this because we have been unable to obtain the proper figures from the government. We have no statistics before us which would enable us to decide that question with any degree of finality.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I never said that unemployment in Montreal had decreased; I said that the unemployment situation was worse during the last campaign than it is at the present time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is worse still.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. minister is not saying it is dark, but he is suggesting it is becoming .very blue. I do not know whether he means Montreal or other parts of the country, but if he has any figures on the matter I would like him to supply them to the house. Judging from my own experience and from what I hear everywhere, I am afraid that the situation, at least regarding Montreal -the hon. minister should be better acquainted with that district than with other parts of the country-is no better. It may be slightly improved due to the fact that Montreal is a city where there is a great deal of seasonal employment. There are many men, not only from Montreal but from different parts of the province, who have been able to secure work as longshoremen or with the harbour commission. That happens every year, but I fancy that there are fewer people enjoying that class of employment this year than has been the case in other seasons. I have been told by a number of men who have called upon me that they are receiving only part time employment. These men who work in the harbour of Montreal have to provide for their maintenance throughout the winter; they have to put by a part of their wages for the next winter. They tell me that they are being employed only part time and are able to earn barely enough to live during the summer season and they are very fearful indeed that the situation will be worse this next winter than it was last year.
If I were to look around me I would find my genial friend, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), who did his very best the other day to overcome the intricacies of the procedure and to remind the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gordon), who is the Acting Minister of Labour, that the situation in his province is very bad. If the government would listen to representations which have been made it would realize that the situation this summer is not any too good. This is so, because of the reasons which I have indicated and which obtain in many parts of the country. It is feared that next winter will be a very severe one.
I do not charge that this is all the fault of the government; I will not fall into the same error as did the Conservatives during the last campaign when they did their best to put the responsibility for a world-wide depression upon the Mackenzie King government. I find fault with the government because its candidates and the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) himself actually promised in the most precise terms that if they were elected they would end unemployment at once or perish in the attempt. That would mean that the Prime Minister would resign and give up any power which had come to him because of that promise. I find fault with the government for not implementing that promise when they know very well that the labour and unemployment situations have not improved. In order to justify themselves before the electorate, in order to give themselves a standing in this parliament, they try to cover up thq situation. They exaggerated the situation last year in order to defeat us, and now they are trying to minimize it to save their faces before the Canadian people.

speechtext: Is the hon. member hoping that unemployment will get no better?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have the greatest confidence in this country, but I must admit that there are times when the country is badly handicapped. If history is studied it will be found that these times, by a very strange coincidence, always happened under Conservative regime.
I will make only a passing remark as to the attitude taken by the Minister of Marine in regard to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Desrochers). I cannot understand how an hon. member who had not seen anything of importance in the prolonged discussion on the financial policy of this country, who had remained so remarkably cool during all the debates which have taken place in this house, should have at once become inflamed and incensed on a
The Budget-Mr. Rinfret

matter like that. I understand why a mention of automobiles may incite a certain degree of regret in the mind of my hon. friend and I listened with deep emotion to the funeral oration delivered by him on the tomb of the departed automobiles of the ministers but I would remind him that if they have not got their cars, they are getting $2,000 per year to provide a few flowers for the tomb of the departed cars. Instead of becoming incensed at the statement which he read to this house, perhaps my hon. friend could find a little solace or solution in his bank book, which should show a balance to the good at the end of the year amounting to $2,000.
However, there is something much more important than the question of whether my hon. friend rides in a government car or in his own, and that is the reference he made to the war cry. We have had presented today in this house the very same situation which has been faced in Quebec for the last ten years. Every time the war cry is discussed in our province-if it were to be discussed to-day it would be the same-it has been raised in the first place by the Conservative party. My hon. friends have only to look behind them to see the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Barrette) who moved that famous amendment. During the last three or four general elections the newspapers which sustain the Conservative cause in Quebec, as well as the Conservative speakers, have assailed the Liberal candidates. What did they say? Did they say that the Liberals were against conscription? Not at all, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in favour of conscription! The hon. member for Berthier and his colleagues say:	When we were in the house
-the Deputy Speaker (Mr. LaVergne) will remember those days-an amendment was suggested to do away with conscription and that awful man Laurier and all those hypocritical Liberals voted against the amendment. When we hear that the Minister of Marine expects us to cross our arms and say: Well, that is true, we were in favour of conscription. We are combated in other parts of the country, and cursed in our own province because it is claimed that we were in favour of it. I say again: I know it. I have had to a certain extent the direction of my party in Quebec, and in the last campaign or in previous campaigns we never intended to bring forward that conscription cry. Every time it has been discussed, it has been brought up by members of the Conservative party trying to place the Liberal party in a false light.
Let me give my own experience. During the last campaign I was travelling through Ontario and discussing the issues of the day.

I am not saying this with any degree of animosity, but my good friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) put questions to me through the press, and when I returned to the province of Quebec I had a whole file of clippings containing questions put by the Postmaster General, by Mr. Boyer, who was so thoroughly defeated by the hon. member for St. Henri (Mr. Mercier), and by other Conservative candidates. What were the questions? I regret that I do not have my file before me, but I can indicate the trend of them. The questions were of this nature; What would Mr. King do if there were a war in Europe? What would your leader do if there were a call for soldiers from the other side? This was inviting us in the most provocative way to discuss these very matters that the Minister of Marine now says we raised ourselves, to save our skins, and it is due to them that we are sitting in parliament to-day. I am going to tell my hon. friends that the moment they drop that sort of thing, the moment they forget about that amendment, the moment the Postmaster General ceases to put any more questions to us, the moment my hon. friend himself raises no more such issues, he may be sure that he will never hear any more war cries of that kind.
Let me remind the Minister of Marine that while, as he says, he did not indulge in war cries, he made promises to his own electorate in order to ensure his return to parliament. It was my great privilege to be sent to a joint meeting in Longueuil at which my hon. friend and I were speakers. A tremendous crowd attended; some had come to hear and others had come to see that we were not heard. It was very difficult to get a hearing at that meeting, but I shall be fair enough to say that my hon. friend also had his difficulties. I was, however, close enough to him that, despite the noise made by some of his friends, and perhaps some of mine, I could hear him quite plainly, and he made a solemn promise to the electors of Chambly-Vercheres. He was discussing the Montreal harbour bridge. If there were a county which had benefited by the building of that bridge, a county that had asked for it for a number of years, it was the county of Chambly-Vercheres. My hon. friend is a clever lawyer and he knew this was going to count heavily against his chances. Do hon. members know what he chose to tell his electors in order to remove from their minds the spectacle of this wonderful bridge that had been given? He made them in my presence the solemn promise-and I heard it-that if he were

The Budget-Mr. Rinjret
elected, he would at once abolish the tolls on the Montreal harbour bridge. I did not expect to have the pleasure of following my hon. friend this afternoon, and my file is upstairs in my office. I did my best, a humble Liberal worker, to be frank with the electorate.
