speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes; I did my best to explain to them why we had to charge tolls on that bridge. I told them that when the bills for constructing the bridge were put through, one objection was raised that if the harbour commission had to bear the whole interest on the cost, this would increase wharfage dues in the port of Montreal, and it was not fair to have those dues charged against products that might come from every part of the world. I could demonstrate that by reading certain papers, but perhaps I would not be allowed to read them. Let me, however, summarize them. I contended it was fair that the interest should be paid by those who used the 'bridge. I remember reading later that the present Minister of Marine had been hailed and applauded by the electors because he had promised them freedom from tolls, and that the then Secretary of State had been hissed because he tried to point out why those tolls should remain for a little while. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien), speaking in the house the other day and referring to some railway branch in his part of the country, pointed out that the then Minister of Railways, Mr. Crerar, had been too frank in stating to the electors that it was not possible to build that branch, while the Conservative speaker had taken the much more facile and easier course of promising it without any reservation. The same situation existed in regard to the tolls on the Montreal harbour bridge. I did my best to exiplain that the tolls could not be removed the next day, but the present Minister of Marine, I am willing to admit, was cleverer than I, and he said that he would abolish the tolls at once. If he does not owe his seat in the house to any question pertaining to the w:ar, perhaps some of those who thought they were going to cross that bridge free of all tolls, felt they might vote for him.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have to deny the
statement made by my hon. friend. Nobody in my constituency, not even myself, said that if we should attain power we wrould immediately abolish the tolls on that bridge. What I said-and I repeat it-was that I was in favour of free bridges in my province and that as soon as the exchequer would permit, we would try to reduce and abolish tolls on our bridges.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In that case I must have been very deaf. If that be true, there should not have been any recriminations on that point, because I am also in favour of abolishing bridge tolls when the exchequer will permit. Whether that means this year or one hundred hence, I do not know. I am going to give some friendly advice to my hon. friend, whom I like very well notwithstanding the fact that we differ politically. It would be well for him to explain the matter to his electorate, because some of them are under the misapprehension that very soon they will be able to visit me in St. James without having to pay any tolls on that bridge.
Another promise that he made to his electors is that if he were elected-and perhaps he knew he might become Minister of Marine- he would build part of the harbour of Montreal on the south shore. That is a rather extensive promise. Maybe he was going to move the elevators that were already erected or build new ones, but he said that he was going to see that the Montreal harbour was built on both sides. Possibly he had in mind that when the harbour was built on the south shore, the tolls on the bridge would not be so important, because nobody would need to cross it seeing that they could transact business on either shore of the river. If I remind my hon. friend of these things in a very friendly way, it is merely because in the first place I was not able to tell him some of them in Longueuil owing to the fact that his friends made such a noise on that occasion that I could not be heard even by my immediate followers around me, and in the second place to show him there is a certain danger in claiming that someone else was elected on a certain pretence unless one is sure he has made his own campaign entirely on the general policies of the country.
In following the Minister of Marine I have been drawn away from the subject immediately before the house, so that there remains little time for me to deal with the budget proper. I differ again from my hon. friends opposite when they claim that they were elected on a policy of protection, or even higher protection, that gives them full mandate to raise the tariff in every imaginable way, sometimes in the most whimsical way, and they are merely following their mandate when they bring before the house such schedules as will be presented to the committee of ways and means. I did think, Mr. Speaker, that when the Prime Minister had raised the tariff on four hundred items in the special session of last fall he had done quite a day's work, and I- thought that at this session, instead of having a general increase of the tariff on many other items,
The Budget-Mr. Rinjret

there might be only certain readjustments. I am sure that if the Prime Minister were dealing with this matter in a business way, and not from a political point of view, not with any desire to favour and satisfy a few of his wealthy friends, he himself would admit, and the government would have to admit, that while there are items in the tariff that can stand an increase, there are certainly other items in respect to which it would be in the public interest to decrease the tariff.
I do certainly protest against this doctrine of protection which says that there is only one way of encouraging industries in this country, and that by raising a high tariff wall. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that by developing trade with foreign countries through trade treaties, as we did during the ten years we were in office, we have given to a large number of the industries of this country an export trade which was more favourable than any benefit that could have accrued to them under the protection of a tariff such as we have now. When the Prime Minister begins to place a tariff on such commodities as oranges or tea or meats, or any other things that are used daily in the most humble homes of this country, I do submit that it is not protection at all. It is either a desire for more revenue or it is merely an aberration. Has any hon. gentleman ever seen in this country a shrub growing tea? I have been travelling a great deal in this country but perhaps I have missed the particular spot where tea-plants are grown in Canada. If there is no tea grown in this country, what is the good of taxing tea? In many a humble home in Canada this very commodity is the daily beverage, and the increase in the tariff on tea will impose a very great burden indeed on some of the humble citizens of Canada. The same applies to oranges, and the same to coal. I realize that the government has tried to satisfy the ever-mounting cry for protection for the Nova Scotia and Alberta coal industries, but until I am shown that that coal can be transported with any degree of economic efficiency to the homes of Ontario and Quebec, I protest against such a tariff, which will not protect Canadian coal and will only have the effect of making Canadian citizens in the central parts of this country pay more for the coal they must use.
I find further fault with the government in connection with all the changes made in the tariff at the special session and at this session. All their decisions in these matters have been based on no information at all except what has- been communicated to the Prime Minister himself or what information

he has drawn from his great source of knowledge on matters such as this. What is the good, Mr. Speaker, of having a bill to create a tariff commission when the whole tariff is readjusted before the commission is given any chance to sit? What is the good of changing the tariff in so many instances, and then, after all that has been done, appointing a commission to offer advice? The Prime Minister might as well say, when he moves his bill creating a tariff commission:	Now
that we have done it all, we will institute a commission to tell us how to do it. The fault I find with this budget is that it is not based on any information secured in any public way. By destroying the tariff commission instituted by the former Liberal administration, the government, if there was any logic at all in the course they took, condemned themselves to delay any tariff changes until the new commission had undertaken its duty of advising the government. But I am afraid that this tariff commission is not at all intended to advise the government, but merely to confirm its decisions after they have been arrived at in the little room where the Prime Minister sits with his colleagues, and where they are supposed to discuss matters of state.
It is intended, further, and this is another objection that I have against the policy of the government, to give to that commission the power to change the decisions of this house. The Minister of National Revenue went very far indeed in the last special session when he put through this house, in a hurried way, a bill which empowered him to change the tariff on certain commodities. We have shown the danger of that, citing the case of glass, on which the government at the special session put a tremendous duty and later withdrew the whole protection.

speechtext:
In reply to my hon.
friend I would say that I do not derive my information from any such propaganda, but from that very good Conservative paper in Montreal, the Montreal Gazette, which said that this question of glass had been a tragedy of errors. I am glad to say to my hon. friend, who is an author, and a very excellent one, that this is another instance where Shakespeare has had a commanding voice in this house.

The Budget-Mr. Willis
Before I sit down I wish to place on Hansard, and have it copyrighted perhaps if my hon. friend desires it, a very simple order in council which shows the dangers of dangling and playing with the tariff inside the council room, and there will be the same danger when the matter is submitted to a tariff commission. On May 5, 1931, the Canada Gazette contained a very remarkable order in council, which reads in part:
At the Government House at Ottawa
Friday, the 1st day o-f May, 1931.
Present:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council
His Excellency the Governor General in Council on the recommendation of the Right Honourable R. B. Bennett, the Prime Minister, for the Acting Minister of National Revenue, is pleased to order that the order in council of the 22nd April. 1931 (P.C. 937) be and it is hereby amended by deleting from the list of products which the Minister of National Revenue is authorized to fix the value of for duty purposes, "potatoes," and substituting therefor "radishes."
Here is the situation, Mr. Speaker. The government had decided to place a certain valuation for duty purposes on potatoes. Then they found that it would not work, and instead of rescinding the order in council and passing a new one, they merely amended the previous	order in council, substituting
"radishes" for "potatoes". In all humility I would suggest that if the government does not know the difference between potatoes and radishes, if they think that a potato is simply an expanded radish or a radish a concentrated potato, they certainly require the advice of a tariff commission. That may be an argument advanced to favour the establishment of a tariff board.
As my time is about up I shall merely repeat what I said at the beginning of my remarks, that is instead of railways, bridges, moonbeams, relief for unemployment and agricultural distress, raising the price of butter by replacing the diabolical product from New Zealand with the angelical product from Australia-if instead of making all these promises the Prime Minister had been courageous enough to say to the electors, "In my first budget to the house I shall tax fuel, I shall tax tea, I shall tax oranges, I shall raise the sales tax from one per cent to 4 per cent, I shall put a tax on small cheques, I shall add to the tax on postal service, and when I have done all that and have received from the humble people of this country more money that I need I shall detax myself by 25 per cent of my income"

I say if my right hon. friend had done all that, not only would
he have been sitting on this side of the house but he would not have been able to complete such a speech before an intelligent electorate.
When the Prime Minister states that he has received a mandate from the people to detax himself by 25 per cent I say he is exercising only one more deception after his deception of last year to the Canadian people. Unlike the Minister of Marine I say that the questions before us are most important, and on behalf of the modest, humble people whom I have the honour to represent and whose interests I am.here to defend, I protest most vigorously.
Mr. ERRICK F. WILLIS (Souris): Mr. Speaker, at this time I am taking the liberty of making certain observations in regard to the problem of wheat in some of its important phases in view of the fact that the sale of our wheat crop is at the present time acknowledged to be the greatest Canadian problem.
The recognition of the fact that the sale of our crop is of extreme national importance is of recent date and has been brought about by the fact that commencing in 1929 the flow of wheat from western Canada to the markets of the world was suddenly checked, with the result that grain growers ceased to purchase in the usual way and general business felt the effect by reason of the fact that the purchasing power in western Canada was reduced over four hundred and twenty-five millions of dollars as between 1928 and 1930.
The government of the day is well aware of the seriousness of the problem, and the Prime Minister stated in London that it was Canada's greatest problem, and the Department of Trade and Commerce has instructed its trade commissioners in all corners of the world to bend their efforts to sell our crop.
For these reasons I am taking the liberty of placing before the house certain fundamental considerations and facts concerning this great problem. I do so, not by way of furnishing a solution, but rather by way of a survey, because I believe that there are many in this house and in this country who do not fully appreciate the facts of the situation. Greater knowledge will lead to a speedier solution, and the more minds engaged on the problem the better for the wheat growers of this country.
In the first place, it might be well to consider the trend of production in Canada during the last five years:
Years	Bushels
1926		 407,000,000
1927		 479,000.000
1928		 566,000,000
1929		 304,000,000
1930		 397,000,000
The Budget-Mr. Willis

The Budget-Mr. Willis

There never was a commodity which could be sold without salesmanship, and every week and every month it becomes more apparent. For instance, in 1928 Argentina capitalized on the fact that they had a crop of unusually high quality, and through salesmanship, ousted Canadian competitors to a large extent from the British market, and opened the doors for their own wheat. If, in Great Britain or any of our markets, salesmanship is consistently brought to bear upon buyers in attempting to sell wheats other than those from Canada, and statements are made to the effect that these other wheats are just as good, then, of course, large amounts of competing wheats will be sold, just the same as a good argument will sell a certain amount of any type of goods. Just recently you have the very specific case of the Prince of Wales advising Great Britain that they must use salesmanship in South America in order to sell their products.
Quality is a great factor in any commodity, but the commodity itself must first be placed in the hands of the consumer or else its quality will not be tested, and its place will be taken by an article of an inferior type which is backed by salesmanship. For instance, .tests have now been made which prove beyond any doubt that the highest type of bread can only be made with the addition of not less than 20 per cent Canadian wheat flour. Experiments were conducted in the grain research laboratory of the Board of Grain Commissioners in Winnipeg, which show that even small additions of Canadian hard wheat exert a marked improvement on the wheats commonly used in Europe, and the degree of improvement is measured by increased loaf volume, better texture, and better quality of bread, in accordance with increasing percentages of Canadian wheat present in the mixture. The degree of improvement obtained therefore is directly related to the amount of Canadian wheat used in the mixture.
If there were available, therefore, in the different trade centres of the world, Loaves of bread on exhibition indicating the tremendous superiority in quality of bread baked from Canadian flour over that of any other flour, then the different places of the earth would hesitate before purchasing flour which would make brown, heavy and unpalatable bread. We must remember that in this particular instance it is a matter of applying salesmanship to an article of universal use, of which much the best quality comes from Canada, and if that article, on those facts, cannot be sold to the bread eaters of the world, then the greatest need of the Canadian people is a course in salesmanship.
tMr. Willis.]
For instance, we all well remember the day when durum wheat was unknown, but when Mark Carleton brought that hardy, bearded, rust resisting wheat from the mountain fringes of Russia and planted it in the dry areas of the western states, that when the first crop was grown it was found that there was no market. Millers did not like it for flour, and bakers stated that good bread could not be made from such flour. Mark Carleton was neither discouraged nor depressed, but set out to make the people appreciate its qualities, and, although he was essentially a botanist, he became in effect a dietician, and by means of recipes and education, and by means of mixing, created through macaroni and other outlets, the tremendous market for this wtheat, and it is now stated that durum wheat covered in 1930 millions of acres of land on this continent. The district from which I come would certainly have been ruined long since had it not been for its discovery by Mark Carleton and the subsequent discovery by him of a market for its .use.
One of our greatest needs, therefore, is salesmanship in the different markets of the world, and any action taken by this government or any other organization which will interfere with the close cooperation which must exist between ourselves and European selling agencies, will be an action which the grain growers of this country will neither forgive nor forget.
It may well be stated that the future of the wheat producer has its bright spots. The population of the world increases 20 million per year, and as the average consumption of wheat for every man, woman and child in the world is 21 bushels, it follows that 60 million new additional bushels of wheat are required to feed the world every year. It is also noteworthy, that while, in the past, wheat acreage has increased on the average of between two and three million acres a year, at the present time it is being decreased, and we find that this year, the acreage decreases in a number of countries are as follows:
Per cent
Australia	 30
U.S.A	 16
Argentina	 [DOT] [DOT]	12
Canada	 8
World movements of grain have been greatly increased in the last few months and the sale of Canadian grain has been very successful as shown by the fact that for the eight-month period ending March 31 last, our exports exceeded those of the same eight months of the previous year by over 61 million bushels.

The Budget-Mr. Willis
We must remember that we have had depressions in regard to wheat before, and it is well to remember that in the summer of 1920 some wheat sold at a price of S4.02 a bushel, and by October of 1922 tihe price had dropped to 96 cents a bushel, which is the most severe decline that has ever been experienced in this country. That decline was followed by one of the largest world crops in 1923 to that date, and yet the returns for that crop cannot be regarded as being unsatisfactory to the wheat grower.
Although the Canadian farmer is the most efficient wheat grower in existence, that efficiency is continually increasing and must necessarily do so, and that increase will be necessarily brought about by better methods, better seed, by the use of fertilizers, by the greater use of summer fallow, and by those various means which, from year to year, are making themselves apparent through the work of our agricultural colleges and departments of agriculture. It must always be remembered that as compared with our real competitors, with the exception of the United States, we are competing under conditions which are vastly better than those in the other wheat producing countries of the world.
A new departure has been inaugurated under which eight new junior trade commissioners are being, or have been sent out to the various trade centres of the world, including also one commissioner at Cairo newly reappointed. All these commissioners have been specially instructed to bend every effort in order to sell the Canadian wheat crop, and, inasmuch as the exports to foreign countries for the eight months' period ending March 31 last have been some 61,000,000 bushels in excess of those for the same eight months in the previous year, it leads us to believe that the trade commissioners, as appointed, are doing us a great and useful service.
Constant improvements in production are being noted. In the past we have had durum wheat, created by Mark Carleton of whom mention has been made, which made a tremendous contribution to agriculture in this country by giving us wheat which would stand up against both drought and rust. Then Charles Saunders created marquis wheat, that tough, early maturing wheat which permitted us to grow it in districts more northerly than ever before. These improvements we have had, and we believe that the great menace of rust will eventually be conquered by the chemists and botanists of this country.
The fact that wheat now can be purchased at a lower price than for many years is not without its advantages, inasmuch as by this
22110-177J
cheaper price the wheat consumption has been increased in various countries, and it is only reasonable to suppose that once these people have commenced eating the products of Canadian wheat they will not desire to discontinue merely because of a slight increase in price.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is always on the wheat horizon that great menace of Russia, but it is very interesting to read the summary of the present situation as indicated by the observations of Andrew Cairns, statistician for the Canadian wheat pool, which are here summarized:
Mr. Cairns spent some time in Soviet Russia in October and November of 1930, and out. lines the reasons for the present large exports as follows:
1.	Considerably above average crop, particularly in the regions near the export outlets.
2.	Practically no winter killing, in place of a high normal.
3.	Unusually favourable weather for both winter and spring sowings, resulting in considerably above average yields.
4.	The undoubted ability of the government to collect grain.
5.	The strict rationing of bread supplies.
Mr. Cairns also indicates that the tendency
towards larger exports will be materially checked by the following factors:
1.	Many sections are overrun by Russian thistles, and crops fluctuate very widely in volume.
2.	Home consumption of cereals is increasing very greatly owing to increasing population and acute shortage of other foodstuffs.
3.	Russian railroads are inefficient and there are not sufficient railroads to carry grain to export markets.
4.	Acute shortage of live stock for animal power will tend to check the increase in production.
5.	There is an acute shortage of skilled workers for operating machinery.
6.	Russia has been selling wheat very much below its real cost of production, and, despite their low standard of living, Russia cannot conceivably continue to export wheat in any volume, at present prices.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Nor can
we.
The Budget-Mr. Willis

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Cairns' seventh reason
is that Russian estimates of increased acreage have in the past not been lived up to. Mr. Cairns sums up by saying:
The inability to date_ to replace the lost animal power by machinery, the failure to provide suitable management, the very grave shortage of skilled workers, mechanics and agriculturists, and the general disorganization, all indicate that the possible results of collectivization are still very far from having been accomplished.
According to the International Institute of Agriculture, Russia's exports for 1928 were only 122,000 bushels, and practically none for 1929. Broomhall states they were 89,000,000 for 1930-31 but this is far above official statistics; many figures are stated for the purpose of gaining political advantage by way of international agreements, even as the exaggerations of the past were used for advertising purposes.
One cannot attempt to gauge the possible effect of the Russian crop, but it must be remembered that they seed about 100,000,000 acres of land on which the yield per acre has in the past varied as much as five bushels per acre, and this variation is almost equal to the world's visible supply.
Experience is now teaching us that by the proper application of trade treaties we can enlarge our markets, with t'he result that, for instance, we have this year, been able to ship to France during the past five months 7,350,000 bushels as compared with 1,821,000 bushels for the same five months of 1930. The milling companies of this country have also their part to play in the creation of new uses for wheat by way of new foods, and by advertising of such new wheat foods in the different countries of the world. And, even though the price of those foods is too high for consumption by most of the people in foreign lands, whose incomes are not great, there is, also, a restricted market for high quality products, and, in each country there are always people who are willing to pay good prices for the food they eat.
I am not of the opinion that there is any patent scheme by which the present difficulty may be overcome, but rather am I of the opinion that salesmanship will always sell a good product, and that the problem being an economic one, and production depending to a degree upon price, it will by that very fact solve itself, but we should, at the same time, hasten the solution.
In my opinion the home market is not a solution, inasmuch as it has not solved the problem for the United States, although I think we would be in a much happier position if we could sell 75 per cent of our crop

within this country and need only worry about the remaining 25 per cent, as is the case in the United States, whereas our local market only absorbs 25 per cent of what we produce.
It is stated by many that reduced production will, on the old economic law, solve the problem, but the production of a farmer cannot be controlled like the production of a factory. If you go to an individual farmer and ask him to cut his wheat acreage 25 per cent, he will at once ask you how you know that the price of wheat next fall is not going to be one dollar per bushel, and he will also ask you as to whether you may not be doing him out of 50 per cent of his profits by such a reduction. You can, however, make out a good case by stating to a farmer that if he will summer-fallow more land he will ultimately produce more bushels at a lesser cost. You may by such an argument, which is really well founded, be able to reduce the acreage.
The world is not suffering from a long period of over-production, but it is suffering from the fact that since life began man has been attempting to supply enough food for the world by growing wheat only to find that by reason of increased rainfall during the last four years as compared with the previous four years the average yield per acre was increased by two bushels per acre on a world acreage of 300,000,000 acres, and produced our present surplus of about 600,000,000 bushels. Without that increased yield per acre we would to-day be facing a shortage of wheat, and it would take very little to place us in that position again. A few inches of rain may nullify the effect of any attempt at decreased production and the lack of it may leave the world's supply of wheat exhausted.
I think the survey as given will indicate that we have a surplus of wheat on hand due to increased production in 1928, brought about by increased rainfall on 300.000,000 acres. It will also show that that surplus in Canada is rapidly being decreased and that in spite of tariffs and other barriers, our wheat is being sold in Europe as never before on a quality basis through the efforts of trade commissioners.
The situation in Russia may change at any time through the fact that their production per acre varies to an extreme degree due to the fact that they are now cultivating poor lands by way of increased acreage. The lessening of production per acre in Russia alone might decrease their crop by an amount greater than the world surplus, and a change in rainfall of one or two inches on the wheat-lands of the world would leave us with underproduction rather than over-production. In the struggle of the survival of the fittest, the

The Budget-Mr. Willis
Canadian grower is the most efficient, has the highest quality product, and can feed himself by mixed farming, and in the end will succeed.
The situation may change from a surplus to a condition of under-production at any time by variation in the amount of sunshine or rainfall which may come from the heavens during this year. Bread even at prices which have prevailed in the last few years is still the world's most. economical food and the chief commodity upon which the commerce of the world depends for life. Finally, it is well to remember that although man cannot live by bread alone, yet millions of the people of this earth are going to continue to eat bread and other products made from Canadian wheat.
I think I should be recreant to my duty if, before I sat down, I did not pay tribute to the most courteous and, in my opinion, most efficient department of the government, namely, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. May I pay tribute particularly at this time, because I got most of my figures from him, to Doctor Grindley who is in charge of the agricultural branch? May I thank at the same time the government of the day inasmuch as in regard to the wheat situation we now have a subvention of five cents a bushel? In Canada we export normally around 200,000,000 bushels annually and if one multiplies that by five cents, one finds it amounts to a gift to the Canadian wheat growers of around $10,000,000. May I also thank the present administration for the duty of twenty-five cents a bushel on corn? I have had occasion previously to discuss in the house the question of corn and barley. May I call attention to the fact that last year we imported 8,000,000 bushels of corn for purposes of feed and that we paid for that corn to Argentina and also to the United States in the neighbourhood of $6,000,000. Now we shall be able to keep their corn out and we have increased to a tremendous extent the market for Canadian barley which needs that market so badly.
May I finally pay my respects to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) whom I regret, is not in his seat? I do this because on two occasions the hon. member did me the honour of giving me some advice in this house. I do not belong to the Scotch nationality and I am not one of those who believe things should not be returned, so I am going, just for a moment, to give some advice to the hon. member for Provencher. I trust I shall not harm him, because he is not. in his seat and it wtould not be right if I
were to do so. But may I explain to the house the great ignorance under which I laboured when I came here? I looked up in the Parliamentary Guide the name of the hon. member for Provencher, and I found there that his party is the "National Progressive Party." When I entered the chamber first,
I looked for the hon. member for Provencher because he comes from my province. I had this idea, rightly or wrongly, on account of his being a National Progressive: I thought first, he being a nationalist, will probably sit close to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr, Bourassa) who, as I understand the matter, leads all the members of the Nationalist party in the house. Then, rightly or wrongly,
I had the further idea that as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) leads the Progressive group in the house, this will place the hon. member for Provencher in a dilemma, but perhaps he will sit between those two hon. members. So I looked for the hon. member for Provencher when I came to the house, and by way of explaining my great ignorance, I was not able to find him in the seat which I expected he would occupy. I expected he would be in the seat now occupied by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), which is the only seat between the two hon. members whom I have mentioned.
I looked around for some time to find the hon. member for Provencher as a National Progressive.. Imagine my surprise when I found him sitting in the second row, right in the centre of the Liberal party! Imagine my surprise when I saw ham sitting in a seat in which normally a cabinet minister*would sit, right iii the heart of the Liberal party! Therefore it seems to me that having been disillusioned in this very abrupt manner, I should give some advice to my hon. friend. May I suggest to him that he approach the hon. member for Battle River and ask him whether he will not vacate his seat in his favour, lest in the house he be done the great injustice of being accused of being a Liberal.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May
I in my opening remarks pay tribute to the last speaker, the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) ? One of the new members from the west, he has already demonstrated an eloquence and an ability to study that do him great credit. I sincerely trust he will continue in the good path he appears to have laid out for himself in studying the statistics of economics at the feet of Doctor Grindley and the bureau of statistics. In time we may hope to find him one of our allies. No real student
2790	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
of economics can ever sit long with the Tory party; true economics and Toryism do not go together.
It is not, however, my purpose in my earlier remarks to deal at any great length with the shortcomings of the budget. As a matter of fact it would probably take me four hours, as it did the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), to do justice to its injustices, but I wish to make reference to some remarks made by the leader of the opposition the other day in regard to our subamendment. It may, of course, be personal prejudice, but I feel that my right hon. friend somewhat spoiled an eloquent and magnificent effort by a determined attempt to destroy the effectiveness of the only concrete proposal that has been put forward from this side of the house in regard to the budget. Let me point out that in so far as the general criticism set forth in the Liberal amendment is concerned, we are in complete accord; we have said almost the same thing in our own amendment. The leader of the opposition agreed with that; in fact he pointed it out to the house, but if hon. members will read the proposals contained in the amendment of the Liberal party, they will find them to be so vague as to be mistlike, wraithlike. They are the ghosts of old Liberal principles wandering around homeless in the guise of an amendment to a budget. There is no specific proposal of any land. Let me remind hon. members of that phase of the amendment.
This house is of the opinion-
Says the Liberal party.
*-that the existing economic depression can only be overcome by policies which are of a character-	.
-to do so and so. Of course, but what are the policies? They do not say. There are no definite proposals with regard to either legislation, treaty matters or anything else; they are merely vague generalities: First, to relieve unemployment; second, to restore to a condition of parity the relation between the purchasing powers of all classes; third, to bring about more equitable distribution of the burdens of taxation; fourth, to encourage the extension of the external trade of the country. As a matter of fact, the Conservative party could vote for every one of those without any difficulty as being mere declarations of an objective. But they could not vote for this last one in their present frame of mind. It reads: "To restore to parliament its full authority over tariff and taxation." I regard that as the only definite point in the amendment. The whole amendment is a generality too vague to be worthy of 
the crisis in which, as the leader of the opposition himself admitted, this country finds itself, and so we found ourselves called upon to move our own amendment.
Before I reach that, let me say this in passing, that I have rarely in this house listened to a speech that so interested me throughout or so held the interest of the entire house and galleries as the speech of the leader of the opposition. It is seldom that any hon. member can afford to devote three, or worse still, four hours to an address in a debate on any subject, and that the right hon. leader of the opposition could do so, and do it effectively, is a great tribute not only to the material contained in his speech but to the manner of his delivery. I pass to our own amendment.
Our own amendment agrees with the Liberals in so far as the general analysis of the crisis is concerned, at least as to the extent of the crisis, but not as to the causes. Then we continue and we propose:
That the present economic conditions demand intelligent and intensive study and definite planning upon a national scale, with the view of substituting well defined cooperative principles in respect of production and distribution, together with the mobilization of our natural resources, technical equipment and financial machinery, in place of the highly competitive system under which we are suffering at the present time.
As it is apparent that these fundamental changes cannot be put into effect in the immediate future, and that the present situation requires some prompt action.
And as the present financial situation is in many respects similar to but more serious than that which prevailed in 1914 at which time extraordinary measures were taken by the government, including the suspension of the redemption of dominion notes in gold:
That is a specific recommendation, and our object in doing that is set forth in the following subclauses:
(a)	Commodity price levels may be raised, thus increasing the purchasing power of those engaged in agriculture, mining, forestry, fishing and other primary industries and in this way promoting a corresponding increase in the volume of employment;
That refers to the primary industries, in whose interest the leader of the opposition was so eloquent. The amendment continues:
(b)	That the burden of both public and private debts and the interest thereon may be lightened;
(c)	That the amount of currency and credit available for the purpose of trade and commerce within the country, may be increased;
(d)	That through the increased volume of
trade thus secured there might result larger revenues without any increase in the rate of taxation.	*

The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
Dealing with that, which was a specific recommendation, having for its objective exactly the same goal that the leader of the opposition himself pleaded we should seek, in his criticism of it the leader of the opposition said that it did not refer to the fiscal policy of the Conservative party, that it did not refer to tariffs, and that in that regard it was unworthy of the hon. members in this comer of the house. In the first place the right hon. gentleman is mistaken. Whilst we do not refer to fiscal policy in so many words, if he would have read with closer attention the very first paragraph of our amendment he would have noticed that it says this:
This house further regrets the proposed decrease in the income tax as applied to the larger incomes as a retrograde step and wholly unwarranted in the present state of the national exchequer and especially in view of the heavy additional taxation imposed upon the consumers of the country.
I do recognize that the tariff has an effect, an evil effect, on the welfare of the consuming dlasses of this and other countries. That certainly is not sufficient reason for the condemnation of our amendment by the leader of the opposition. We propose something besides platitudes. We propose something besides what the budget proposes, which, in effect, if I may generalize it, proposes relief for the rich at the expense of the great masses of the consuming people of this country. It may be described as a budget which is calculated to gratify the cold-blooded, callous creators of a condition of enslavement of the masses of the people of this country. Mr. Speaker, this and other countries, if I read aright the authorities on economic history like Doctor William B. Munro of Harvard and others, ever since democracy pretended to function, have been in the hands and under the control of the financial class. The evolution of the political and economic conditions within the state have been consistently dictated by organized wealth. Professor Munro himself in a magnificent article in the Atlantic Monthly not many years ago made that statement, and it is as true to-day as it was then. Mr. Lloyd George, speaking in regard to the Dawes plan, now discredited, and which was the great production of those financial rulers whom governments follow said:
Agreement would never have been reached without the brusque and brutal intervention of international bankers. They swept statesmen, politicians, jurists and journalists all on one side, and issued orders with the imperiousness of absolute monarchs who knew that there was no appeal from their ruthless decrees. This settlement is the joint ukase of king dollar and king sterling.
The condition under which this country and the world to-day suffers is the direct result of following out the same ruthless, brutal and callous policy of king sterling and king dollar.
Hon. members to my right in this debate are inclined to stress the importance of fiscal policy. The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) nods his head in approval. I shake hands with him on that. Fiscal policy, is immensely important to the well-being of any country-immensely important-but fiscal policy, even free trade at this moment, cannot remedy the existing situation, and I will show why before I get through. I do agree to this extent, that the fiscal policy of this administration is one destructive of national interests, destructive of international amity, and destructive of foreign trade, but behind it all there is a gleam of hope because it is destructive of the veiy party that is responsible for it. They cannot long sustain themselves in office with a policy of this kind in the face of existing conditions throughout the world and against the advice of every economist of standing in the world to-day. But let me, on the other hand, retort to my hon. friend from Weyburn and those enthusiasts who ignore other factors and concentrate their attention on tariffs, to this effect, that in spite of the existence of what they were then pleased to term prohibitory tariffs throughout the world in 1928 and 1929, the existence of those tariffs did not prevent the tremendous flood of alleged prosperity that swept over all of North America and even over other parts of the globe, but principally North America. Why was it that prosperity was able to sweep across this continent and had its effect and repercussions throughout the world? Prosperity came, in spite of protective tariffs, because at that time there was a policy of credit relaxation and there was a flow of currency into the blood stream of the commerce of the nation. As my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) has just said, there was deliberate inflation, an inflation to which if carried to excess my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) very properly takes exception.
While I am on that point may 'I assure my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre and my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Geary), who spoke the other night in criticism of our proposal, that the very last thing we would suggest would be any policy of inflation. What we are recommending is a policy of anti-deflation. We are recommending a policy of depreciated exchange, an altogether different
2792	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
policy from that of inflation. In Germany there was inflation-wild, uncontrolled, and followed by serious results. In France there was controlled inflation. The franc had depreciated under unguided inflation to a serious point. But a point was reached where the statesmen of France determined they were going to stabilize the franc, and they were successful in their efforts. The prosperity of the country was restored, internal debts were paid off, and the satisfactory condition of France is now well known throughout the world. France was in a comparatively prosperous condition through all that period in 1920 and 1021 when the rest of Europe and we on this continent were suffering so in matters both of trade and of finance. Only recently has France begun to experience the repercussions of the distaster which has come upon the rest of the world.
I say therefore that tariffs, protective or otherwise, are not the fundamental cause of present problems. I agree with men like Mr. Neill of the Royal Bank, and for once, even with Sir Herbert Holt-just imagine how he must feel about it-and others, that the principal cause of the present condition in this country and throughout the world is a wrong monetary policy. If hon. members were to consult yesterday's newspapers they would find in one of them a statement made by Sir Basil Blackett, one of the directors of the Bank of England. I would like hon. members to notice how radical he is becoming. Even the Tory members opposite might recognize the respectability of what I am saying when men like Sir Basil Blackett are in accord. Sir Basil Blackett is quoted as follows:
The basic cause of the present difficulties lay in the banking methods, in a too rigid gold standard and in the monetary policy generally.
Note the words "in a too rigid gold standard." Could anything be more definite than that, coming from an authority of that type?-"a too rigid gold standard" that has placed world commerce in a strait-jacket. The gold standard is doing what strait-jackets can be made to do, namely, acting as a ligature which has a repressive effect upon the whole blood stream of the body politic. Sir Basil Blackett attributes the difficulty to a too rigid gold standard and monetary policy.
Then Sir Josiah Stamp steps in and states that the difficulty lies in the inability to control or regulate internationally, gold and credit distribution. He continues-and with all due respect I ask my hon. friends to my right, because I think there is some hope among them, to listen to this:
Many of our troubles would pass if bankers- 
And may I add, statesmen.
only could be weaned from their traditional beliefs.
I ask my hon. friends to note that phrase,- "could be weaned from their traditional beliefs." Until we reject the gold mentality, in the face of existing conditions there is no hope for general trade recovery. At this stage I cannot do better than to refer to men such as Gustav Cassel, than whom there could be no more distinguished witness, a man who was retained by the League of Nations to make an investigation into the causes of the deflation period of 1920 and 1921. He is reputed to be one of the greatest economic authorities in Europe. At that time Gustav Cassel made the following statement, which is as true to-day as it was then:
The downward movement of prices has not, as is sometimes assumed, been merely a spontaneous result of forces beyond our control. It is entirely the result of a policy deliberately framed with a view to bringing down prices, and giving a higher value to the monetary unit.
That was the effect in 1920 and 1921, and it is the effect to-day.
Now, if you please, the chief objection to our proposals from the great Liberal, the leader of the opposition himself, is that it would be a measure of fraud. I must state that he did not use the word "fraud" but I have no doubt that is what he meant. He suggested that if our proposition were carried into effect it would perpetrate a fraud upon those who had recently subscribed to the new conversion loan and expected payment in gold. In effect he said that if we were to adopt this new policy as set out by hon. members in this corner of the house we. should have made an announcement to the public before the conversion bonds were issued to the effect that they would not be payable in gold. I say that If the right hon. gentleman had studied the question a little closer he would have found that many of the bonds which were being converted in the first place were not made payable in*gold; many of them were not. For that reason no fraud has been perpetrated upon the bondholders and our proposal would have the effect of restoring to the people that which has been taken away from them by the fraud of deflation. Gustav Cassel has said:
A prolonged fall of prices must necessarily have an extremely disturbing effect upon production and trade.
Obviously that statement is as true now as it was when it was made.
I now turn to another authority which was quoted with great pleasure and satisfaction a few years ago by the Minister of Trade and

The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
Commerce (Mr. Stevens), Mr. J. M. Keynes a well-known British economist and authority who says "deflation"-and that is what we have to-day-
Deflation involves a transference of wealth.
I ask hon. members to note this statement:
Deflation involves a transference of wealth from the rest of the community to the rentier class and to all holders of titles to money.
That, of course, includes bonds and bondholders. The leader of the opposition thinks it would not be fair to accept our proposal, even after we have been forced to give everything by way of reduced prices and increased purchasing power of moneys and bonds. The value of those bonds was advanced enormously through the deflation policy of the banking fraternity. I continue the quotation:
Tn particular it involves a transference from a)ll borrowers to lenders.
I repeat that, "a transference from all borrowers to lenders"-of wealth. Our debts as primary producers have been doubled in terms of our products.
It is unfortunate that Lord Milner died, because he was reaching the very height of his effectiveness as an advocate of the new economics. Lord Milner said:
Just as productive industry welcomes raising prices-
The very thing we must have, if there is to be restored prosperity in this country or throughout the world-
Just as productive industry welcomes raising prices the moneyed interests must always be in favour of falling prices, because they render its own wares-money-more valuable.
We have referred to authorities such as Gustav Cassel, Lord Milner, Blackett and others and equally as expert authorities are scattered throughout North America. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that if Benjamin Strong, one of the greatest minds in the banking circles of the United States of America, had only lived I venture to say he would have been strong enough to prevent the political policy of the federal reserve board from almost destroying the trade of the world. I do not think there is a single student of this subject that will be willing to release the federal reserve board of the United States in particular and the other cooperating central banks of the world in general from direct responsibility for the world conditions.
Going back for one moment to this question of tariffs, I want to make clear what my own position is. I say-and my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) may enjoy this part of it-I say that the world could become
quite accustomed to, and even make progress, under moderate tariffs. Yes-if they were stabilized. Just as when you fix a ligature around an artery or a vein the natural process begins to operate and transfer the blood stream into the other smaller channels, which gradually expand in order to take up the abnormal flow, and only a temporary effect is created. The member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) can explain that better.

speechtext: The effect is permanent on that spot, but the general effect is not. The general healthy condition and usefulness of the part can be restored- unless they do what my hon. friends opposite are d'oing and ligature every blood stream.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would bring death.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is exactly what it is doing-it is bringing economic death, it is bringing trade stagnation, and their policy can do nothing else but that. I ask my hon. friend to read what Sir George Paish said in an interview reported in the New York Times of June 9. He points out that the world is facing complete destruction to-day if the nations continue to obstruct by restrictive tariffs the channels through which the blood stream flows. Trade is not the blood stream, the blood stream itself is finance. Without that little will move. The body politic cannot operate without the flow of the blood stream without credit, without the necessary purchasing power in the hands of the people of the nations of the world. You have in this country and in otheT countries a state of economic war that followed the physical war, brought on by the narrow economic nationalism of selfish trade patriots who do not possess sufficient economic intelligence to realize the madness of their proposal. The nations of the world have all been guilty of this folly

yes, almost all of them with perhaps the one exception of Great Britain; she has refused to be tied up to this strangling and crazy policy. May I venture to remark that I would not be at all surprised to find that Great Britain would be the first nation to recover. She will recover first because she will not be faced with the same restrictions in the way of the free flow of credit and the free flow of goods.
I have said in passing that in spite of a moderate tariff we might succeed, we might progress. But neither this nor any other country can make progress, even if the blood stream of credit is ample, in face of the obstruction to external trade. We might
2794	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
have a measure of well-being under such a condition of isolation, but I doubt it. I doubt if isolated we could even be prosperous, but certainly we would not progress in proportion to the progress made by the other nations of the world under those conditions. It is as insane to starve the nations of the necessary blood stream of credit, purchasing power, money, call it what you will, and to restrict the channels through which resulting trade can flow, as it would be for each of us individually to tie ligatures around every important artery and vein in our system and so prevent the flow of life-giving blood to the various organs-just as insane. As a result of these fiscal policies throughout the world we are sick umto death. Sir George Paish points it out in telling language. Let m'e give his words; they are too effective to pass over. He said:
World-wide economic disaster oan now only be mitigated, it cannot be avoided.
Why, of course it cannot; it is here; we are in the midst of it-the greatest economic disaster the world has ever seen in my lifetime. Sir George Paish continues:
In a measure, we are going to fight probably the greatest peace battle tliaf we have fought. You will remember that during the war we were right up against it. We had to mobilize all our forces to win the war. Now, we have to mobilize the forces of every possible kind to win this fight against trade depression. Indeed, if I may say so, in my judgment there is a danger, a great danger, of a complete breakdown of trade, and we must be prepared.
But, Mr. Speaker, this country stands in a strange position. Are we lacking in sufficient intelligence to be able to take the initiative? This proposal of ours is not a new thing; it has been done before, and done effectively. When war was declared, what happened? The bankers rushed down to Ottawa and saw Sir Robert Borden and Sir Thomas White, and a meeting of council was called. They sat all night. What followed? Next day a law was illegally altered in the interest of the banks so they might not be required to redeem their notes in gold. Of course, later that illegal step was legalized That action was taken to meet a national emergency. We are confronted with a national emergency to-day. We are faced with more poverty, more destitution, more bankruptcy than ever we had at that time.
I think it was Maurice Colbourne who said that war was economic peace and that peace brings economic war. We are facing a war condition to-day. Yes, unfortunately through our administration, in part, and through the

policies of the various narrow, nationalistic governments throughout the world we have economic warfare as intense and destructive as physical warfare. The wheat growers and the other primary producers of this country are struggling for their very life in the face of a trade war with countries that are in the favourable position because of depreciated exchange of being able to sell goods at prices below ours. All we ask is that you give the wheat growers a chance. I say to the government:	Since you assert willingness to give
all Canadians a chance, give the Canadian farmer a chance. Five cents a bushel! Well, the manner of introducing the five-cent-a-bushel proposal indicates the lack of thought given to it. I am satisfied the Prime Minister cannot have sat down in cold and solemn consultation with himself, or with anybody else, to find out what that five cents means to the farmer.

We all recognize your

speechtext: Are we to regard that five cents a bushel as a compensating adjustment for the losses that result to us under the new tariff, under the sales tax, under the other taxes that this government has imposed upon us?-for primary producers like the farmer must carry the great load of taxation. The primary producers are the only great class in the community that cannot pass on the load of taxation to somebody else. We pay freight both ways; we buy retail and sell wholesale; we buy at a protected price level and sell in the competitive markets of the world.
