You don't know the
ABC of economics.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon.
gentlemen opposite are getting prodded where they do not like it. Now, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister offers us five cents a bushel on our wheat. If that is to be regarded as a compensating adjustment, I reject it, I do not want it. It cannot be regarded as a compensating adjustment. If it is a measure of direct relief, if it is a dole, then we have to accept it, for that is the position in which western agriculture is to-day. The western farmer has reached the position

The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
where even doles are acceptable to carry him through the period of penury that is facing him, notwithstanding the promise of the Prime Minister to blast a way to the markets of the world for his products.
The right hon. leader of the opposition was guilty of one thing for which I was sorry; he used a purely Tory argument against our subamendment. He said we were not sufficiently enlightened in regard to this gold standard subject.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Probably he spoke the
truth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hon. members in this corner, and economists-from whom my hon. friend opposite might take a lesson-have been trying to get politicians and statesmen to study the problem for the last fifteen years. We' in this part of the house have been trying to study it for the last nine years. We are offering to you what suggestions we can of a constructive character in this crisis; you have not a single one of your own. These tariffs, bounties, subsidies and bonuses are all hopeless, uneconomic and unworthy of intelligent economists, who do not sanction them. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the leader of the opposition will not be satisfied merely to say there is no general consensus of view which is accepted. Why, the general consensus of economists to-day, with one or two Tory exceptions perhaps-like Professor Swanson, who might not like the gold standard to be abolished, and a few others-is in favour of the modification of the gold standard. The majority of international economists today such as Gustav Cassel, Maynard Keynes, Professor Irving Fisher and all those other people, are satisfied that we must meet -this present crisis upon some basis other than the monetary system based upon gold.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What other basis do you
suggest?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is all in our amendment; I have not time to repeat it now. Why should the parliament of Canada take the initiative? I will tell you why. Canada is facing a depression such as we have never faced before, and why should not we in this new country, fresh, virile, vigorous and courageous, have sufficient internal stamina to take the plunge? We cannot be any worse off; economists show us that we will be better off. More than that, even the leader of the opposition must know, as a student of economics, that there cannot be any general recovery in trade until the volume
of credit and currency in this and the other countries of the world increases. How far should it increase? It must never increase beyond the point of absorbed production. It can be regulated; it can be more intelligently regulated than the world has been able to regulate the gold standard. The gold standard never has regulated the vo'ume of currency permanently in favour of the people; it has brought attenuating fluctuations upward to the benefit of the speculative classes, and then downward to increase the wealth of its controllers.
Let me just give this one illustration from an article on "Credit Control" by Professor Curtis; this will illustrate my statement that you have wild and uncontrolled inflation, under the gold standard:
Current loans in Canada, which were well below a million in 1925 and 1926, increased to a maximum of $1,473,000,000 in 1929; call loans in Canada which in 1925 were running around the $100,000,000 point increased to $280,000,000 in 1929; call loans elsewhere than in Canada, which in 1923 and 1924 were below the $200,000,000 mark, increased in 1929 to over $330,000,000. Total loans in Canada, which were around the $1,100,000,000 mark in 1925, amounted to $1,856,757,000 in October, 1929. From this it can be seen that there was a large absolute growth in all classes of loans. . . . And that it caused .... "a substantial price inflation in Canada and the virtual abandonment of the gold standard."
Of course it did. The advocates of the gold standard abandoned it during the period of prosperity through which we have just passed, and after it had carried North America to that peak of production the federal reserve board policy, following the election of Mr. Hoover in the United States, burst the bubble and crashed the whole thing down about our ears.
I am sorry I have not much time left, because there is much more that should be said in connection with this matter. Let me do my best once more, in pleading, to ask hon. members of this house not to shut their minds to the certainty that reform of our present monetary system is essential before there can be general trade recovery in this or any other nation of the world. You must always have a volume of purchasing power in circulation in any nation sufficient to take up the volume of production within the nation at any given time. That volume of currency should never exceed the volume of production, nor should the volume of production ever be permitted to exceed the volume of currency. On the one hand you have deflation and on the other hand inflation. That matter surely can be regulated; we can regulate almost every other matter.
2796	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
It can be done, and it must be done. Mr. Neill, of the Royal Bank, is no faddist or crank; he says it can be done and must be done. Other authorities to-day are saying the same thing.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do not be afraid.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was only afraid I could not give my hon. friends a little more of the same thing. The leader of the opposition was perhaps at his best when he described the economic feudalism into which the policy of the present administration was thrusting this country. I share his opinions in that regard; I think he is absolutely correct in his analysis, but I ask him this: What does he think of the financial feudalism we now have, which is more effective, more feudal in character, more enslaving than the economic feudalism of which he spoke so eloquently? Our boasted freedom is but a myth. We can talk about our political status; it is all right; it makes good talk. We can talk about the evil of annexation, Mr. Speaker, but the effective annexation of this country took place long ago. We are the tail of the United States dog to-day, and we wag as the dog wishes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take it back.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I have order, please, Mr. Speaker? Let me tell you this-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a nice thing for a Canadian to say.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will tell you that so long as hon. gentlemen opposite and hon. gentlemen to my right permit the federal reserve board of the United States of America to dictate the financial policy of this country, we are just wagging as directed; that is all. Mr. Neill of the Royal bank, my indignant friend-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Neill never made any such statement as that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Neill did make the statement that the federal reserve policy is chiefly responsible for this depression in Canada, and he is not the only one. The principal economists of this and other countries place at the door of the federal reserve system the responsibility for existing world conditions. Is my hon. friend proud of the fact that the banking policy of the United States of America has brought Canada
LMr. E. J. Garland.]
to this depression? What I want to see is a Canada free; I want to see us declare our own monetary policy. I am not, as hon. gentlemen. are, blinding my eyes to the existing conditions. I ask them that we should dictate our own policy and go off the gold standard. Let us create our own credit for our own purposes, as we need it, and we will help build up a prosperous country. We will never make it prosperous by a restrictive policy of fiscal tariffs a strait-jacket of gold and nothing else.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before the hon. member
takes his seat, would he mind giving us his definition of purchasing power?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am afraid I would need another forty minutes for that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the budget. Were I to do anything else I would be recreant to my duty to the province which gave me birth, and to the people whom I have the honour to represent in the parliament of Canada. In the maritime provinces, in respect to our greatest and most basic industry, that of coal, it is conceded by Liberals and Conservatives alike that this budget was the best budget for the province of Nova Scotia ever brought down in this house.
I shall deal, in a few minutes, with the budget in its application to Nova Scotia, but before doing so may I follow briefly the arguments presented by the official critic of the Liberal party, my good friend the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). May I at the outset congratulate my hon. friend upon the distinctive honour which his right hon. leader conveyed upon him when he selected him to be the critic of the Liberal party in so far as this budget is concerned, but when I do convey to him my congratulations I must mingle with them my sincere regret that that political preferment which he obtained from his leader was obtained by sacrificing and betraying the interests of one quarter of the population of his native province.
His first argument, if argument it might be called-1 think perhaps instead of using thi3 contention he should have allowed it to be used by the other financial critic of the Liberal party, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), namely-that the budget was late in being brought down. Perhaps it was, but we have had two budgets within a little over six months. I desire to reecho his words throughout the province of Nova Scotia. We all know that but recently my hon. friend shook the dust of his province from his heels

The Budget-Mr. Macdougall
and settled in the city of Montreal. When he was in Nova Scotia his plea used to be for the downtrodden and oppressed, for the agriculturist, for the fisherman, for the miner, and so on, but why does he protest against this budget being so late? He is looking through the umbrae and shades of big business in the city of Montreal and he protested in the interests of big business of this country.
His second argument, if it can be dignified by that term, was that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was not doing right in occupying the dual position of Prime Minister and Minister of Finance. The official leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) reechoed that statement in his very admirable speech delivered the other day. He spoke about Gladstone in 1880, but, I believe, had he gone further in the very book from which he was quoting he would have found that the official critic who criticized Gladstone at that time because he occupied these two positions was defeated at the next general elections in England. My right hon. friend may have had in his mind his colleague the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth. Let me assure him that if that hon. gentleman ever enters Nova Scotia, that little province which he loved and left, seeking reelection to parliament, we will be minus his bland and smiling countenance when the election is over.
My hon. friend, the official critic of his party, then referred to the Imperial conference. He said that the Liberal party were trying in every conceivable way to make it a success. How were they trying to make it a success? My right hon. friend said that he had locked himself up in the fastnesses of Kingsmere in order that he might not embarrass the government. He said nothing and did nothing, and as we all know, of nothing nothing comes. No success was ever made out of nothing. Let the impartial readers of the records of this house read the speeches delivered by my right hon. friend and his supporters on the address and I am confident that they will come to this conclusion, that there was a studied attempt on the part of the opposition to create in this country an atmosphere of prejudice should the Imperial conference sit in the capital city of our dominion

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend
wants to ask a question let him stand up in his place and do so, but he should not subject this house to the groans and grunts which five thousand years ago ceased to be the language of humanity.
Anyone who is unbiased, reading the speeches of my hon. friends, will come to
the conclusion that there was a studied attempt, on the part of hon. members of the opposition, from their right hon. leader to his humblest supporter, to create an amosphere of prejudice should that conference sit in the capital city of Canada. It is not going to sit.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It will lie and die.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They say it ought
to sit anyway. Australia and New Zealand cannot send their delegates to the conference, yet my hon. friends opposite say, have that conference this year. We are going to have a conference next year with all the component parts of the empire represented for the first time in the capital city of our country.
The next point raised by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth was in regard to the withdrawal by New Zealand of the British preference, and hon. gentlemen opposite have had the audacity to say that this action was occasioned by an amendment introduced by the Conservative party when in opposition. What are the facts? If there ever was a man who paraded this country deriding orders in councils, it was the right hon. the leader of the opposition, but by an order in council his government extended to New Zealand the same conditions which prevailed under the Australian treaty. It is a misnomer to call it the New Zealand treaty, because there never was a treaty; there was an order in council. The two points about this New Zealand arrangement are these; either that arrangement was good or it was bad. If it was good, my right hon. friend's govemement should never have given notice to New Zealand that they were going to abrogate it; if it was bad my right hon. friend's government should never have passed the order in council. But they did both; they were not content with getting on one horn of the dilemma, they got on both horns. The statement that we were in any way responsible for the action taken by New Zealand is mere eyewash. That action was taken because of an injudicious order in council passed by my hon. friend's government which drove a coffin nail into the dairy industry of Canada. When the dairy industry had to protest in order to survive, then my hon. friend gave a six months' notice for the abrogation of that agreement.
The next point I will refer to-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friena a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not
ready to answer a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend next dealt with the Canadian National Railways,
The Budget-Mr. Macdougall

and in that subterranean method which has been employed by the Liberal party during recent years, he tried to make out that the Conservative party was opposed to the Canadian National system. Why? Because the Conservative party, mindful of its duty to the taxpayers of this country, wanted an accounting of the financial transactions of the Canadian National Railways. That railway is the people's road and it is paid for by the people's taxes and we have a right to know what is going on. No man in this country can be adjudged an enemy of that system who wants to have the facts made known for the benefit of those who pay the shot. But if there be any party in Canada that should never raise its voice above a whisper in regard to the Canadian National Railways, it is the party led by my right hon. friend opposite. Older parliamentarians than I in the house will remember the strenuous efforts made by my right hon. friend and his party to prevent the formation of the Canadian National system. If anybody desires proof of this, let him turn to Hansard of the second session of 1919, volume 2, and he will find it there in abundance. When the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, supported by every Conservative in the house, was attempting to put through the formation of the Canadian National Railways; when he was putting through this first great experiment in public ownership, he was bitterly opposed by the official opposition. One amendment after another was introduced, and if hon. members will look at Hansard of that date at page 1746, they will find one of the most ridiculous amendments ever introduced in any parliament in any part of the world. I have not at my disposal the time to read it all, but I shall read some of it. It was moved by Mr. Parent, and a part of it reads:
That the ownership by the Canadian government of the American section of the Grand Trunk railway would involve this country in international troubles respecting labour administration and public policy;
That for the above-mentioned reasons, the acquisition of these lines means a serious danger of the annexation of Canada by the United States.
If hon. members look at the yeas, they will find the name of my right hon. friend who to-day leads the Liberal party. No sooner was that amendment defeated than the late lamented James Robb moved that the bill be given the six months' hoist, and the name of my right hon. friend will be found in support of that motion also. The point about the Canadian National railway system is this, that the Conservative party, instead of being the enemies of public ownership in this country,
fMr. Macdougall.]
were the people who brought public ownership into being, and the Liberal party were the people who tried to prevent it.
The leader of the opposition then went on to tallk about expenditures and he criticized the government because their expenditures were too great. He said that they were expending $430,000,000, while last year the Liberal administration had spent only $440,000,000.	1
mention this just to show the utter lack of consistency on the part of my hon. friend, because immediately after making the statement that we were spending too much money, he turns around and in a very hostile manner criticizes the government because they were not going to increase their expenditures by paying 100 per cent old age pensions.
In regard to old age pensions, what is the situation? We all know the act which was passed under the administration of my right hon. friend and under which the provinces would have to pay 50 per cent of the cost. The provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, being the older provinces, and having, in regard to population, a larger number of aged people than the other provinces, were unable to take advantage of the act as it stood. My right hon. leader has promised the people that the federal government will sustain this burden. At the present time, in the bitter economic straits in which not only Canada but the whole world finds itself, it is impossible for him to do this now, but he has shown his good faith by increasing the amount to 75 per cent. Already a leader in public life in Prince Edward Island has notified the people that that offer will be accepted, and as far as Nova Scotia is concerned I feel quite certain that offer will be accepted until such time as the federal government may find itself in a position to bear the total burden resulting from old age pensions. What is the position now of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth? What is the position of the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Usley)? What is the position of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff)? They are supporting an amendment which will make it impossible for the old men and old women of their native province to get this old age pension. Ever since this question became a live issue in 1925, they have played polities with grey hairs in Nova Scotia. No longer will they be able to do that. They introduce an amendment to-day which, if it passes this house, but which of course it will not do, will make it impossible for the old people of Nova Scotia to receive this need of social justice.
I wish I had some little time to. devote to the excellent speech of the leader of the

The Budget-Mr. Macdougall
Liberal party, but unfortunately I have less than forty minutes at my disposal. There were some high lights in that speech. My right hon. friend is making quite a reputation as a marathon orator. He spoke for four hours and thirty minutes on the address and for four hours and ten minutes on the budget. I wish to draw this to the attention of hon. members whose notice it may have escaped, because I think it may amuse them:	After
my right hon. friend had been speaking on the budget for four hours and five minutes, and making a very excellent address, he started his peroration. Let us remember that my right hon. friend is a man of great educational ability; he is a man who has occupied an outstanding position in Canadian public life; he has been Prime Minister of Canada for ten years; he represents a certain element of public opinion in this country and many thousands of people were waiting for this statement of his. Knowing the difficult situation in which Canada is at present in common with every other country in the world, they were anxious to learn his solution for the problems that confront the dominion. They had a natural right to do that and to think he would offer some constructive criticism. If hon. members will turn to page 2710 of Hansard of this year, they, will find the beginning of his peroration. After he had spoken, mind you, for four hours and five minutes, he has this to say:
If I may I should like to conclude with one constructive suggestion.
After speaking for four hours, he admits puiblicly to the people of Canada that he cannot give them anything that will be of assistance in ameliorating their condition or in solving their problems. But what was the constructive suggestion that he gave? It was that a board should be appointed, composed of almost every element in the population, to deal with unemployment. It would take about a year to get such a board constituted. This session of parliament would be over long before such a board would be set up, and when it was constituted, a remedy for unemployment must necessitate the spending of money. This board, therefore, would be called upon to spend money, and my right hon. friend, who is so strong on the constitution, would take away from parliament and from the government control over expenditure and taxation and vest it in the hands of an irresponsible board. If that suggestion were made on our side of the house, would my right hon. friend not go up and down the countiy raising a new constitutional issue?
May I now come to the last part of the speech of the official financial critic, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, in connection with the coal industry of the province of Nova Scotia. I noticed how little time he devoted to that, how his eyes were fastened on the clock, and I felt sorry for my hon. friend; for I felt at the time that he was sacrificing his native province because he wanted to do a service to his party.
He started in by telling us that he would welcome any tangible assistance to the coal industry of the province of Nova Scotia, and then immediately after that he moved an amendment that would make it impossible for this tangible assistance to _ be given to the coal industry of Nova Scotia. He then proceeded to quote an old Latin adage, and I think before I get through he will be sorry that he ever mentioned this proverb. It was a proverb that became current in Rome in the time of Nero, "Equi donati dentes non inspiciuntur"-do not look a gift horse in the mouth. This proverb dates back to the time of Nero in Rome, and you all know that Nero fiddled while Rome burned. My hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth will be remembered by future generations of Nova Scotians as the man who fiddled while the Conservative * party and the representatives of the Conservative party from Nova Scotia were trying to put through this house the best measure of assistance that has ever been accorded to the Nova Scotia coal industry.
But may I proceed further with that proverb. If my hon. friend will look up G. L. Apperson's English Proverbs he will see that the proverb he quoted the other day became current in England in the fourteenth century, and in 1674 there was a great pageant in which different proverbs were exemplified for the edification of the people. In that pageant a man came out riding a horse backwards, and they put into the mouth of this buffoon the words, "I ride in this manner with my face to the horse's tail that I may make good the truth of the proverb, Do not look a gift horse in the mouth". So I think my hon. friend very unfortunate in selecting that proverb when he started to denounce the coal provisions of this budget which have been brought down to assist the coal industry of Nova Scotia.
I want to call this to the attention of the house for the edification particularly of the Halifax Morning Chronicle, an organ that has a very high regard for my hon. friend, and for the edification of the leader of the Liberal party in the province of Nova Scotia, my esteemed opponent in the last election, who
The Budget-Mr. Macdougall

is now going up and down the province of Nova Scotia in the interests of national unity, I suppose, telling the people that Ontario and the other provinces are crushing the lifeblood out of Nova Scotia, and that they can get nothing except by fighting for it. Yet ' my hon. friend the leader of the Liberals of Nova Scotia in federal politics, stands in his place and says that what we get for the coal industry of Nova Scotia in this budget is a gift from the rest of Canada. I entirely disagree. There is no gift involved. What this government has done has been simply to do belated justice to that great coal industry in the province of Nova Scotia, justice which the government of my right hon. friend opposite was either unwilling or afraid to do. That was the position in regard to the coal industry.
My hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth said, and I suppose the wish was father to the thought, that these measures taken to protect the coal industry of Nova Scotia and to extend our sales in the market of Canada and give more employment to our 13,000 miners, would not .mean the movement of sixty thousand tons of Nova Scotia coal. My only reply to that is that he does not know what he is talking about. Take anthracite screenings, for example. Anthracite screenings from the United States were supplied to the province of Quebec alone to the extent of 250,000 tons. Authorities on the coal industry in Nova Scotia, and some of them are Grits, tell me that as a result of the new duty we can capture that market for Nova Scotia soft coal. I need not detain the house with a further discussion of this subject, which has been very ably dealt with by my good friend the Minister of Fisheries in an estimable speech, except to say that I believe that with the assistance that has been given to the coal industry of Nova Scotia by this budget the industry -will have a chance to supply 800,000 tons a year more of Nova Scotia coal than we did before.
There is one other point in the speech of my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth to which I wish to allude, and that is the conversion loan. My bon. friend is a hidebound Grit. He cannot see any good politically in anybody who is not a Grit, and he could not even give any commendation to the government for its success with regard to the conversion loan. As a matter of fact, he tried to damn it with faint praise. He would have had us believe that it was a very ordinary transaction, something that anybody could do, something of no importance. Let us turn back to the past for just a [Mr. Macdougail.l
moment, to the year 1923, when the Liberals started to put through one of these very ordinary transactions, a conversion loan. At that time a good grey head from the province of Nova Scotia, who has since gone to his eternal reward, was finance minister in this country, a man who had made a distinctive place for himself in his native province and in the dominion, a man who had earned for himself by splendid traits of heart and mind the affection and esteem of his fellow-Canadians in every part of Canada. I refer to the late lamented Right Hon. W. S. Fielding. What did this great Canadian Minister of Finance have to say in his budget speech presented on May 11, 1923. At page 2542 of Hansard of that date, dealing with the question of loan operations, he has this to say:
The loan operations of the last year are partly known already to the house. I mentioned last session the New York loan of $100,000,000. The five-year bonds at 51 per cent, 1917 victory loan, amounting to $182,834,500, matured on December 1, 1922. The holders of these bonds were given the privilege of exchanging maturing bonds-
Here is what my hon. friend calls an ordinary transaction:
-for new bonds bearing 5J per cent interest-
The same rate of interest as the old ones:
-and taxable as follows: Five-year bonds due November 1. 1927; ten-year bonds due November 1, 1932. The holders of the maturing bonds took advantage of the offer to the extent of ' $114,449,250, leaving a balance of $68,385,250 to be redeemed in cash.
There is the result of their conversion loan.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did my hon. friend take
notice that those were five-year and ten-year bonds, not twenty-five and thirty-year bonds?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That makes it all
the worse. Did my hon. friend notice this, that the Fielding conversion loan carried the same rate of interest as the old bonds to be retired, while the conversion loan of my right hon. leader paid one per cent less than the bonds that were being converted? He asked for $250,000,000 and got 8640,000,000. The Liberal party asked for a conversion loan of $182,000,000 at the same rate of interest, and it was under-subscribed 33 per cent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was only a short term loan.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That may be a very ordinary transaction, but to my mind it is proof positive of something I knew before-' that the Liberal party is not capable of doing even a very ordinary thing.

The Budget-Mr. Turnbull
I have not much more time at my disposal, but there are one or two further points to which I should like to refer. In speeches such as that of my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) we have heard a great deal of pessimism, groaning and croaking about conditions in this country. May I say that I have the greatest confidence in Canada, in its resources, in its people, and in the courageous man who leads its government. When men at this admittedly difficult time of our nation's history, a time which might be termed difficult in the history of any nation, go about with wringing hands and running noses preaching the philosophy of despair, they get no sympathy from me, because I do not think that type of psychology will help Canada in its present economic difficulties. As the descendant of a highland Scot may I be pardoned if I prefer to give my allegiance to a man such as my right hon. leader, who has shown, as has no other leader in Canadian public life, the virtue of courage-courage, as Sir James Barrie once termed it-"the lovely virtue; the gift of himself that God gave to His children." I prefer to follow the leader of the house and not those who preach pessimism and suggest nothing. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that this country is not bankrupt; we have resources, and we have men of ability. Canada will emerge triumphantly from this temporary depression, and sooner than any other country in the world.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I shall not vote for the subamendment, I shall not vote for the amendment, but I shall vote for the budget, because I think it good.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, probably I ought to apologize for taking part in the debate at such a late hour. There have however been things said during the progress of the debate which affect the particular portion of the country from which I come. Statements have been made which to my mind should be corrected before the conclusion of the debate.
I listened with a great deal of attention to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) the other afternoon and evening. I heard him call upon my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) to declare his principles in such terms that the people of Canada would know exactly where he stood on public questions. I had thought there could be no person within the borders of Canada or for that matter of the British Empire who did not know exactly where the right hon. leader of the government stood on all public questions.
I had hoped that when the right hon. leader of the opposition was begging his opponents to declare their principles, he himself would have done his duty by declaring the principles of the party he leads. I am prompted to say that by reason of statements which have been made within and without the walls of the house. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) speaking in the house on June 10, is reported at page 2492 of Hansard in the following words:
Throughout the last election campaign the Prime Minister on many platforms in the country advocated a tariff which would admit of competition and equal opportunity for producers within our own country. I do not think any hon. member could find a great deal of fault with such a tariff.
In fact I might go a little further and say I would be a little bit inclined to favour the Canadian producer over the foreign manufacturer.
There we have evidence of what might be called a fair example of the protectionist sentiment rampant within the ranks of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition.
At page 2502 of Hansard appears a statement by the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan). I quote as follows:
Never were truer words spoken than those of the British chancellor of the exchequer who said: Once begin a policy of protection and you are on a slippery slope which leads to a bottomless pit.
I wonder if the hon. member for North Waterloo appreciates the direction in which he is heading. I wonder if the right hon. leader of the opposition will advise this house as to which of those two policies he purposes to follow, whether he is going with the hon. member for South Huron into the bottomless pit, or whether he will follow the principles of protection advocated by the hon. member for North Waterloo.
Out in my native province, of Saskatchewan other principles are being preached. We are told by the Liberal leaders in the province that the Liberal party throughout Canada is one, and that the provincial party represents Liberal thought in Saskatchewan. On February 4, 1931, Mr. T. C. Davis, the Attorney General under the Liberal government of the province of Saskatchewan, referred to the Dunning budget as "the first step in the carrying out of the five year plan for free trade with Great Britain as an exemplification of the resolution passed by the provincial legislature that year." I would ask my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, on the first occasion which presents itself, to say to the people of Canada in tones that Canada may



The Budget-Mr. Turnbull
hear, and in clear definite language incapable of double interpretation, where his party stands, so that when next we go to the country there will be a clear issue upon which we may get a clear-cut positive decision.
In the province of Saskatchewan there is a gentleman named Mr. George Spence who was at one time an hon. member of this house, and who is now Liberal organizer in that province. On February 4, 1931, Mr. Spence, speaking in the legislature of the province of Saskatchewan, is quoted as follows:
In reply to a question across the floor of the house from Premier Anderson the speaker intimated that he was in favour of free entry into Canada of goods from Germany, Japan and Russia. He proceeded to declare that the race for increased tariffs which had been pursued in the world was now over.
I would ask my right hon. friend as early as possible to tell the people of Canada if his organizer in the province of Saskatchewan truly represents Liberal policies in Canada, so that the people of Ontario, Quebec and the rest of Canada will know whether or ndt he is in favour of free trade with Germany, Japan and Russia. I think the right hon. gentleman owes the country and his party a statement to clear up this point. In justice to the voters of Canada a statement should be made at once containing a clear declaration of principle from the right hon. gentleman.
The question has been raised in this house as to whether the tariff provisions of the present government have resulted in the establishment of new industries in Canada, and the suggestion has been made that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister was not correct when he stated that about 87 industries had been brought into this country. Perhaps my hon. friends opposite will take the word of a gentleman outside of Canada who is not politically interested in the fortunes of any Canadian political party. I place before hon. members of the house a statement by William Philip Sims, foreign editor of the Scripps-Howard press, writing in the New York World-Telegram. I quote the following:
Profiting by America's blunder, Canada today aims at nothing less than making herself perhaps the greatest manufacturing and exporting nation in the world,-greater than England and greater than the United States.
The newspaper comment continues:
Mr. Sims promises to tell of one single American industry that has lost 22,000 jobs to Canada since Premier Bennett came into power.
Surely that is worth something to the people of this country. Discussing Canada's aims Mr. Sims is further quoted as follows:
[Mr. Turnbull.1
No less than 107 important concerns established branches on this side of the boundary in 1930, more than doubling the 1929 exodus and quadrupling the number that migrated in 1928.
Compare those figures with the figures quoted by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard). He stated that from 500 to 700 new industries were supposed to have been established in this country in 1929 and 1930. Compare them with the figures given by the right hon. leader of the opposition in his speech the other day, when he said some 300 new industries had been established along the main line of the Canadian National Railways in 1930 alone. These gentlemen well knew that they were not talking of industries coming in to this country from other parts of the world, but of little industries established here and there by Canadian capital venturing to come out into the open and set up industries of their own. Mr. Sims continues:
No less than 107 important concerns established branches on this side of the boundary in 1930, more than doubling the 1929 exodus and quadrupling the number that migrated in 1928.
And the rush continues.
Canada is extending an open invitation to American industry to establish plants on this side of the line, and her inducements are
many;
1.	Location in a country that is closer both to Europe and the newly awakened Asia by several hundred miles than is the United States, and with only a slight disadvantage in reaching the twenty republics of Latin America;
2.	Cheap and plentiful hydro-electric power, as indispensable to industry to-day as was coal yesterday-power over which the government keeps strict control;
3.	An unsurpassed base for foreign trade, with the benefits of preferential rates with the other members of the British empire and special trade relations with twenty-three other foreign nations;
4.	Her own expanding domestic market.
I may add that the figures that were quoted by my right hon. leader are confirmed by the bureau of statistics. I have the figures before me, but I will not quote them to-night.
In my own city of Regina we find already some benefits from the policies of this government. All last winter the local General Motors plant stood idle, but in the spring of this year the discount rates on imported automobiles was changed, and as a result that plant started operations again, and the last news I had was that 520 men were at work and that the plant was making greater sales than had been expected.
The duty on corn is a benefit to western Canada, for it will assist our farmers to dispose of their barley crop. If my hon.

The Budget-Mr. Turnbull
friends opposite from the province of Alberta had looked more carefully through the tariff they might have found some reductions, for it is not purely a tariff of increases; in it will be found several items now on the free list that were subject to duty under the Liberal regime. The placing of those items on the free list is going to be of assistance to industries in Saskatchewan.
Then there is the assistance to wheat. I understand that some of my hon. friends opposite are a little troubled about this assistance given to the wheat industry. We have heard in this house from time to time of a number of new industries having been established in the eastern provinces which would to a very large extent take care of unemployment in those parts of the dominion. That benefit to the east must be balanced by something that will take care of unemployment in western Canada, and there is nothing that will do so more effectively than giving a fair price to the people of western Canada for the things they produce. When the western farmer gets his remittance of five cents a bushel on his wheat I do not think he will thank the member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) for the scoffs and sneers with which he greeted that proposal in the budget.
In my constituency a new experimental station has been established by the Department of Agriculture for the purpose of dealing with two great troubles of the farmers of Saskatchewan-soil drift and the cutworm.
Some reference has been made to the public debt. We are told that under the Liberal regime it decreased by a considerable amount. I believe that to be true. We are also told that under the Liberal regime the Canadian National debt, which is really part of the public debt, increased very largely. There has been some discussion as to how much of the national debt is war debt and how much is ordinary debt, and the question has been raised whether there should not be a sinking fund established to take care of its repayment. I should like to see the national debt divided into three columns: first, ordinary debt; second, war debt; third, railway debt. That information should be published every time the national debt is referred to, so that our people will not be misinformed regarding the exact standing of the three great divisions of the debt for which the country is responsible. Then I should like to see a sinking fund established to take care of the war debt. I believe our people would be willing to bear a pretty heavy taxation if they were satisfied their taxes were going to repay the debt in-
22110- 178J
curred during the four years of war. If a sinking fund could be established for that purpose,and special taxes levied to retire that particular debt, I feel confident that the people would wholeheartedly endorse such action. It might be a little difficult under present conditions when revenues are low, but in a few years when we get back to normal I think that step should be taken.
I have heard a good deal during this debate in regard to the sales tax and the tremendous burden it is supposed to impose on the common people by its having been increased to 4 per cent. I am not so much afraid of that result as some hon. members appear to be. I was talking the other day with a merchant on Sparks street who is in the clothing business. He told me that he had received a new price list from the manufacturers soon after the budget was brought down, and that that price list will absorb so much of the sales tax that his company will be able to sell their goods to the people of Ottawa at no increase in price. I have also a statement from the manager of one of the large mail order houses in the city of Regina that their goods will not be increased in price in consequence of the increased sales tax, that the tax will all be absorbed before the goods reach the consumer. With the present depressed prices and the keen competition for business, I feel quite satisfied that while some part of the added sales tax may reach the ultimate consumer, the major part of it will be absorbed by the manufacturer and wholesaler.
We heard something the other night with regard to gasoline. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) regaled the house with a long list showing the profits the oil companies made during the regime of his right hon. leader. That right hon. gentleman while in opposition railed against trusts, combines and mergers, but his voice was strangely silent for the nine long years he was in power while trusts, combines and mergers flourished in this country as they never had before in our history. They made considerable profits during the nine years that the Liberal party was in power. Apparently they are making some profits to-day. But my hon. friend from Swift Current would have been fairer to those companies if he had told the house that during the period between September of last year and the day he was speaking the price of gasoline in Saskatchewan had been reduced by four cents a gallon. He did not tell us that. I understand a similar reduction took place over the whole of Canada. So instead of taking $24,000,000 out of the pockets

The Budget-Mr. Turnbull
of the farmers of Canada the oil companies put $24,000,000 into their pockets. On the very day the hon. gentleman was speaking the newspapers published the further information that the Imperial Oil Company Limited -which he was reviling-had reduced the price of tractor kerosene by five cents a gallon. That kind of kerosene is used by the farmers in operating their tractors. Gasoline is what motorists use in their automobiles, to run up and ' down the highways, but the farmer is much more interested in tractors than in automobiles. The Imperial Oil Company has also announced a reduction of 15 per cent in the price of lubricating oil for these tractors.
The hon. member for Weyburn, speaking in the house the other day, declared that our trade had fallen off by $300,000,000 last year, and that the average duty on imported goods was 26 per cent; that 26 per cent on $300,000,000 was just $78,000,000; and that that was exactly the amount of our deficit. He tried to lead the people to think that this deficit was arrived at by taking 26 per cent of the reduction in our imports. The bureau of statistics will tell you that if you take the wholesale prices of goods in 1926 at 100 per cent, the wholesale prices of goods to-day represent 73 per cent. That is, there has been a reduction in the wholesale prices of 27 per cent since 1926, and I venture to say that all of that reduction has taken place since 1930. That 27 per cent practically coincides with the falling off of the imports and exports of this country. I am inclined to think that it is not a question of falling off in volume, but rather of price, and that the volume of our trade with foreign countries is just as well sustained to-day in spite of the depression as it was in the palmy days of 1929 and 1930. Later in his speech he stated that the average was 30 and not 26 per cent. One of my hon. friends to-day, who wished to be a little more exuberant than the hon. member for Weyburn, announced that the average duty was 33 per cent. That is the way they talked in western Canada. Mr. Speaker, and that is why the farmers of that country have so long been deluded by this free trade talk. That is why they had an exaggerated idea of this tariff and what it means. As a matter of fact the average duty on goods coming into this country is not 33 per cent, or 30 per cent, or even 26 per cent; the average rate is less than 15 per cent bn the whole amount of goods imported.
I thought it my duty to place these facts on record so that the people of western Canada as well as the people of the east might know exactly the facts in regard to these matters dealt with by my western friends. I thought perhaps the right hon. leader of the opposition,

having it called to his attention, might take the first opportunity to tell western Canada *whether he is in favour of free trade with Great Britain in five years, or whether he is in favour of free trade with Germany, Japan and Russia right away, so that there will be no delusion in western Canada as to where the Liberal party really stands.
This budget has regard for the essential needs of the country; by building up a prosperous Canada it will promote our own welfare and that of the empire, and for that I propose to support it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it my duty in this debate to speak on behalf of the citizens of Laprairie-Napierville and state, as it is within my province to do, what they believe to be in the 'best interests of this country. Of course I do not intend to say anything new on this budget. It has been discussed by both sides of the house in a very interesting manner, and as far as I am concerned-and I believe I interpret the sentiments of hon. members on this side-my right hon. chieftain has said all that could have been said in regard to this matter. Nevertheless, as a representative of the people, I think I should say a few words on the budget.
I am glad to congratulate all the hon. members who have taken part in the debate on both sides of the house, and particularly I should like to congratulate the ex-Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) who so well described and characterized the sentiment we all feel, particularly in the province of Quebec, with regard to the budget presented by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). I remember that when I studied the history of the world, one of the reasons given for the American revolution was this slogan: "No taxation without representation." That was about a century and a half ago, 'but to-day in this very country it is our duty to repeat the same words in this chamber: "No taxation without representation."
As the hon. member for St. James said this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, hon. members to your right went around the country during the campaign making speeches and promises which no men who had any respect for themselves would have dared utter on public platforms. So far as the citizens of Laprairie-Napierville are concerned, they understand the public questions before the country at the present time; they read every day what goes on in connection with the great problems which are now facing Canada. I repeat that no man in this country with any self-respect would have dared say to the citizens of Canada such things

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis
as were said by the Prime Minister in the last campaign, knowing that he would be unable to fulfil his promises, just for the sake of winning power. During the last campaign the right hon. Prime Minister was only a candidate for the position he now occupies; he Was anxious to become Prime Minister and believed that he would derive great pleasure from doing so. I would remind him of what Constance Bennett said with regard to a similar situation:
I have learned from life and experience that pleasure is transient.
My right hon. friend, in passing from the position of leader of the opposition, must find himself in a difficult situation, and he must be convinced, as was Constance Bennett, that pleasure is transient, realizing as he must that it is no pleasure to occupy his present position.
I come now to the fiscal policy of the Conservative party, not of the present party but of the party of days gone by, to use the words of the Prime Minister. Is the policy of the present Conservative party similar to that of their predecessors? I dare to say that it is not. Where is there a leader of the Conservative party who made such drastic changes in the tariff as did the present Prime Minister during the special and present sessions? It is unnecessary for me to repeat the policies of Sir John A. Macdonald, of Sir Robert Borden and of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. That has been done ably by my right hon. leader, but I should like to quote from utterances made during the electoral campaign of 1921. At that time Mr. Meighen was speaking about the fiscal policy of the Conservative party, and I dare say he was very anxious to bring about a situation which would meet the interests of the people of Canada in general. Speaking in Hamilton on September 1, 1921, presumably in answer to the leader of the Liberal party, Mr. Mackenzie King, after first explaining his general policy, Mr. Arthur Meighen, as quoted in the Montreal Gazette of September 2, 1921, said:
Nor has all this been accomplished by insistence on a high protective tariff.
Apparently in an effort to defend himself against the charge of believing in a high protective policy, he said:
Quite the contrary. For years back our tariff has ranged around 16 per cent on the total of goods imported. It is now less than 15 per cent. Our duty on dutiable goods alone averages under 22 per cent, the lowest since 1878, the lowest indeed of any considerable country in the world save Great Britain alone and I doubt very much if it is higher even than Great Britain will be under the tariff that has just passed their House of Commons.
That is the declaration made by the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen when he was speaking on the tariff and apparently in reply to the charge made against him that he was the gramophone of Mackenzie and Mann. He then said:
The man who talks of the tariff of Canada being a high tariff-especially if he is a man who maintained a higher tariff himself when we did not need a tariff half as much-that man, I say, is a humbug.
That nickname came from the mouth of Mr. Meighen. He said that the man who propounded a high tariff is a humbug. Is it permissible for me, Mr. Speaker, to say that the first man to give that name to the right hon. the Prime Minister is not Mr. Thomas of London, but his predecessor, Mr. Arthur Meighen?

Generally speaking, I do not like to speak from sentiment, but I should like to follow that great Liberal chieftain who is named in history as the leader of our cause, of our system and of our liberty. What is said with respect to this budget? Speaking for the people of my county and
2S06
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis

also, I believe, for the people of this country in general, I think I have a right to say that this budget is not a popular one. I am sorry that this budget has been presented by the Prime Minister. I have a great respect for the right hon. gentleman; I have a great admiration for his talents and experience as a business man. But I believe he is overburdened with the responsibilities that he has voluntarily assumed. He holds three positions: Prime Minister, Minister of External Affairs and Minister of Finance. This is too much for any one man, and I believe he was unable to take time to pause and consider the interests of the people in general. I think he is acting in good faith in bringing down this budget, but had he had time enough to pause and reflect upon the future of this country, upon the interests of the people in general-and I am here to speak for the common people-he would not have put upon the record of the house such a speech as the one he made upon the- first of June.
I shall not recite the series of taxes that have been thrown on the shoulders of the citizens of this country, and, in particular, the citizens of my county. The citizens of my county are composed of farmers and workingmen. During the last campaign the farmers were promised by the Conservative candidates and their friends that if they gave their confidence to the Conservative party, they would have a paradise on this earth; they would sell their eggs, not at from thirty-five to forty cents a dozen as they used to do prior to the election, but at from fifty to seventy-five cents a dozen; they would sell their butter, not at forty-five cents a pound, but at a much higher figure, they would sell their potatoes-and the people of my riding are potato growers-not at $1 but at 12 a bag, and they would sell their other vegetables at proportionately higher prices. But, thank heaven, the citizens of my county were not so easily deceived by these demagogues; they voted against them, and to-day if it were possible to open my constituency of Laprairie-Napierville, when the electors see that their eggs are selling at fifteen cents a dozen at the stores, their potatoes at fifty cents a bag, their butter at fifteen cents a pound, and their cream-because the citizens of my county sell their cream on the Bonsecours market-at five gallons for $1.50, I do not believe ten per cent of the electors of my county, whether Liberal or Conservative, would vote for the government at present in power.

Hon. members opposite laugh at that, but the people of this country, who are the people of their own country, are not laughing; they are crying. Last Saturday, to be precise, a lady came into my office. Hon. gentlemen opposite laugh at that. They should not laugh; it was an old lady. Hon. gentlemen cannot stop me by laughing. I remember reading in history that when Disraeli was making one of his earliest speeches in the House of Commons of England the members laughed at him, but they did so only once because they saw in Disraeli

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis
a man who was working for and giving his life for his country. And so do I-I am speaking on behalf of my people. This old lady came to see me about her husband, who had been employed for fifteen years in the same position on the Canadian Pacific Railway, but who was then out of work and had been unable to obtain employment since December, 1930. This man had six children who he was unable to provide with the necessaries of life, and this old lady asked me to try to get a position for her husband. She told me that one of her children was sick in the hospital and that she was unable to buy the drugs and medicines that were needed. It was not until she came to speak of her sick child and began to cry that I realized how discouraged she was. I am unable, of course, to finance all the poor people who are made even poorer by the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite, but I did not look at my balance sheet; I gave her enough money to buy the drugs she needed for her sick child. Laugh now if you are able to laugh. Where is the man among you who would not have done the same thing to help relieve the misery of a poor old lady under such circumstances?
But that is only one instance, Mr. Speaker. If you go and observe the work of the religious and charitable institutions in Montreal, even right now, in the summer, you will see as many as a hundred people in a line waiting their turn to get soup and bread-and hon. gentlemen on the other side laugh when I speak of that. speechtext:
Before the debate proceeds further, I wish to refer to an incident that occurred this afternoon. The hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau), referring to a statement reported to have been made by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Des-rochers) outside of this house, characterized the same as "a lie, an absolute lie, a tissue of falsehoods, more than a lie, made with the deliberate intention to deceive."
The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) raised the point of order that such expressions were out of order.
The hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), opposing the point of order, pointed out that the statement so characterized by the hon. minister was not made in this house, but was made outside.
At the time I was of the opinion that as the expressions were applied to a statement made outside this house, they were not out of order. However, I have examined precedents and the English and Canadian authorities and find that I was probably in error. May, at page 325, says:
It is not parliamentary to accuse a member of misrepresentation or to charge him with falsehood.
Bourinot, at page 364, says:
Or to say of a member that he stated what "he knows not to be correct," and such statement must be withdrawn.
At page 362, Bourinot says:
Or to say of a member he went about the country telling palpable lies.
Some of these expressions are milder than the words in question, some are about on a par, but all are held to be unparliamentary. Therefore, in order that decorum in debate in this house may be maintained and that my ruling referred to may not be a precedent for departing from decorum, I am bound to say that in my considered opinion the words, "a lie, an absolute lie, a tissue of falsehoods, more than a lie, made with the deliberate intention to deceive," are unparliamentary, notwithstanding the fact that they were used in reference to a statement made outside this house, and I ask the hon. minister to withdraw or modify them.
